## Project Agency — Q167
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately preserve knowledge that would enable its own replacement while restricting access to that knowledge?

**Yes. An institution may legitimately restrict access to succession-enabling knowledge when disclosure would create unjustified risks. But those restrictions must not give the institution exclusive authority to determine whether its own replacement is possible, necessary, or legitimate.**

Q166 established that an institution has a defeasible responsibility to preserve meaningful pathways for its replacement.

That responsibility does not require immediate replacement.

Nor does it require sacrificing essential functions merely to demonstrate that the institution could disappear.

But succession often depends on knowledge.

A successor may need records, technical understanding, institutional history, procedural expertise, and evidence concerning unresolved obligations.

Some of that information may be sensitive.

Some may concern people who never consented to its disclosure.

Some may enable capabilities that should remain subject to authorization.

And some may reveal institutional vulnerabilities.

The resulting dilemma is straightforward:

> **An institution may need to restrict knowledge to govern responsibly, yet unrestricted control over that knowledge may allow it to prevent legitimate challenges to its own authority.**

The problem is not solved by declaring that transparency is always good or secrecy is always necessary.

It requires a theory of legitimate epistemic custody.

---

### 1. Knowledge preservation and knowledge disclosure are different duties

Suppose institution I possesses records essential to its operation.

Those records would allow a legitimate successor J to understand how I performs its functions.

Does I have a duty to publish them?

Not necessarily.

Preserving information does not require distributing it to everyone.

A record can be retained securely.

It can be made available to authorized reviewers.

It can be transferred under defined conditions.

It can be summarized without disclosing protected details.

It can be subjected to independent verification without being publicly released.

These arrangements differ significantly.

We should distinguish:

**Preservation:** maintaining information so it remains available for legitimate future purposes.

**Access:** permitting specified parties to inspect information.

**Use:** permitting information to guide particular activities.

**Transfer:** moving custody or operational responsibility to another party.

**Publication:** making information broadly available.

The legitimacy of one does not establish the legitimacy of all the others.

**An institution may have a strong duty to preserve knowledge without having a corresponding duty to disclose that knowledge indiscriminately.**

### 2. Five dimensions of succession-enabling knowledge

Knowledge required for institutional succession is not homogeneous.

| Dimension | What it enables | Constitutional concern |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical knowledge** | Understanding earlier decisions and obligations | Accountability |
| **Operational knowledge** | Maintaining essential functions | Continuity |
| **Evaluative knowledge** | Assessing whether existing procedures work | Independent judgment |
| **Constitutional knowledge** | Understanding authority, challenges, and succession rules | Legitimate governance |
| **Sensitive knowledge** | Accessing protected information or consequential capabilities | Privacy, security, and misuse risks |

A single record may belong to several categories.

For example, an operational log might reveal both why a decision was made and confidential information about affected people.

The categories are analytical distinctions, not necessarily separate files or databases.

Their purpose is to prevent an institution from treating every form of knowledge as though it required the same access policy.

### 3. The epistemic custody problem

Suppose I controls the information needed to determine whether I should be replaced.

I also controls the information needed to carry out replacement.

I claims that disclosing either category would be dangerous.

Who evaluates that claim?

If I is the sole evaluator, the arrangement is vulnerable to capture.

I may be genuinely protecting legitimate interests.

But it may also be protecting its own authority.

And the two motivations may coexist.

This is **epistemic custody under institutional conflict of interest**.

The institution possesses relevant expertise and responsibilities.

Yet it also benefits from controlling the evidence that could justify transferring its powers elsewhere.

The constitutional challenge is to preserve legitimate restrictions without allowing the custodian to become the exclusive judge of their necessity.

### 4. Secrecy can protect agency

We should not assume that restricting information is inherently contrary to legitimate agency.

Suppose institutional records contain private information about affected agents.

Unrestricted disclosure could undermine their ability to control personal information.

Suppose certain operational details could be used to interfere with essential services.

Publishing those details could threaten the very people whose interests the institution exists to protect.

In such cases, disclosure may reduce rather than increase meaningful agency.

The relevant principle is not universal openness.

It is justified control over information.

**Transparency is constitutionally valuable when it improves meaningful assessment and accountability. It is not automatically legitimate when it exposes others to avoidable harm.**

This matters because constitutional analysis can become simplistic when it treats all restrictions as evidence of domination.

Some restrictions protect the conditions under which agency can be exercised.

### 5. Secrecy can also manufacture dependence

Now consider the opposite case.

Institution I refuses to document its procedures.

It keeps essential knowledge concentrated among a small group.

It prevents independent evaluators from examining its performance.

It argues that no successor could operate safely because no successor possesses the necessary expertise.

But the expertise gap exists partly because I has prevented knowledge transfer.

The institution then cites that gap as evidence of its indispensability.

This is **epistemic entrenchment**.

**Epistemic entrenchment occurs when control over relevant knowledge is used to preserve institutional authority by making independent assessment, legitimate succession, or practical alternatives unnecessarily difficult.**

The problem is not simply that information is restricted.

It is that the restriction undermines the conditions for justified governance.

### 6. The difference between protective secrecy and entrenching secrecy

We need a diagnostic distinction.

**Protective secrecy** restricts information because disclosure would create independently assessable risks to legitimate interests.

**Entrenching secrecy** restricts information because disclosure could enable justified challenges to incumbent authority.

In practice, motives and effects may overlap.

An institution may sincerely believe that secrecy protects essential functions while also benefiting from the resulting dependence.

Therefore, subjective intention cannot settle the question.

We should examine:

- the evidence supporting the restriction;
- the consequences of disclosure;
- the consequences of nondisclosure;
- the availability of less restrictive alternatives;
- the independence of review;
- the institution's willingness to permit authorized succession.

The relevant question is not merely why the institution says it restricts access.

It is whether the restriction remains justified when its effects on accountability and replaceability are considered.

### 7. A legitimate restriction must have a defined purpose

Suppose I classifies all operational knowledge as confidential.

Its explanation is:

> “Disclosure might be dangerous.”

That may identify a concern.

It does not establish a sufficiently specific justification.

A defensible restriction should identify the protected interest.

Is the concern privacy?

Security?

Integrity of essential services?

Protection of confidential relationships?

Avoidance of unauthorized use?

Different purposes justify different restrictions.

A privacy concern may support removing identifying details.

An operational concern may support limiting access to qualified parties.

A constitutional concern may require independent review rather than public disclosure.

**The scope of an information restriction should correspond to the legitimate risk it is intended to address.**

Vague danger cannot justify unlimited epistemic control.

### 8. Access should be distinguished from authority to act

Suppose reviewer R needs to inspect records to determine whether I's authority remains legitimate.

Does R therefore need permission to operate I's systems?

No.

Access to evidence is not the same as authorization to exercise the capabilities described by that evidence.

Likewise, an authorized successor may need operational knowledge that an ordinary reviewer does not.

This gives us three distinct permissions:

**Permission to know:** access information for a legitimate purpose.

**Permission to evaluate:** assess evidence and produce consequential judgments.

**Permission to act:** exercise operational or constitutional authority.

These permissions may overlap.

But they should not be conflated.

An institution can support independent evaluation without granting unrestricted operational control.

It can also transfer operational responsibility without granting the successor authority over unrelated functions.

### 9. Independent verification without unrestricted disclosure

Suppose I possesses sensitive evidence relevant to a constitutional challenge.

The evidence cannot responsibly be made public.

Does that mean the challenge cannot be evaluated?

Not necessarily.

A legitimate arrangement might permit appropriately authorized independent reviewers to inspect the evidence.

They may assess whether I's claims are supported.

They may communicate findings at a level of detail compatible with legitimate protections.

They may identify limitations in what can be publicly established.

The arrangement must still be scrutinized.

Reviewers may be captured.

Their access may be selectively restricted.

Their conclusions may lack practical consequences.

But the possibility matters.

**Public disclosure is not the only form of epistemic accountability.**

The stronger requirement is that relevant evidence can be assessed through pathways sufficiently independent of the institution whose authority is at issue.

### 10. Verification must be more than institutional reassurance

Consider a weak arrangement.

I declares:

> “An independent reviewer has confirmed that our restrictions are necessary.”

But I selected the reviewer.

I determined which evidence was available.

I prohibited disclosure of the review's standards.

I retained unrestricted authority to reject the conclusions.

The word *independent* is doing an impressive amount of unpaid labor.

The arrangement may not provide meaningful accountability.

A credible review process requires attention to several dimensions:

**Selection independence:** whether reviewers can exercise judgment without improper incumbent control.

**Evidentiary independence:** whether they can access relevant information rather than only selected material.

**Methodological independence:** whether they can apply appropriate standards of assessment.

**Consequential independence:** whether justified findings can materially affect decisions.

No arrangement guarantees perfect independence.

But each dimension matters.

### 11. The constitutional significance of interpretability

Suppose I preserves every record required for succession.

The records are complete.

They are securely stored.

But nobody outside I can understand them.

Has I satisfied its responsibility?

Only partially.

Information can exist without being usable.

A successor may need explanations, documentation, contextual knowledge, or means of validating interpretations.

This introduces **epistemic transferability**.

**Epistemic transferability is the capacity for relevant knowledge to be understood and appropriately used by legitimate parties other than its current custodian.**

Preservation without transferability may protect historical evidence.

It may fail to preserve meaningful succession.

This is especially important when institutions depend on tacit expertise.

Some knowledge may be difficult to articulate or transfer completely.

That difficulty should be recognized honestly rather than treated as proof that the incumbent must govern forever.

### 12. Tacit knowledge and institutional dependence

Consider a specialized institution.

Its members possess experience that cannot be fully reduced to written procedures.

They understand unusual cases.

They recognize patterns.

They know which formal rules require contextual interpretation.

A successor may lack this knowledge.

Does that justify preserving the incumbent?

It may justify careful transition.

It may justify training, overlap, supervision, or staged delegation.

But it does not automatically justify permanent institutional control.

We should distinguish:

**Irreducible expertise:** knowledge that genuinely depends on experience or context.

**Transferable expertise:** knowledge that can be taught or documented with reasonable effort.

**Institutionally withheld expertise:** knowledge that remains inaccessible because the incumbent has failed or refused to support transfer.

These categories matter because different forms of dependence create different responsibilities.

### 13. A successor must not inherit knowledge without accountability

Suppose I transfers operational knowledge to J.

J can now perform the essential functions.

But J lacks legitimate authority.

It does not accept inherited obligations.

It has no meaningful review procedures.

Is the transfer successful?

Not constitutionally.

Technical competence is insufficient.

Succession must preserve relevant responsibilities and governance arrangements.

Knowledge transfer should therefore be connected to authorization.

The question is not simply whether J can use the information.

It is whether J may legitimately exercise the powers that the information enables.

**The capacity to perform an institutional function does not establish authority to govern that function.**

This principle becomes especially important when knowledge itself enables consequential action.

### 14. The danger of informational monopoly

Suppose I controls four things:

1. The records needed to evaluate its performance.
2. The standards used to interpret those records.
3. The information needed to construct alternatives.
4. The authority to decide whether alternatives are legitimate.

This is a highly concentrated epistemic arrangement.

Even if I acts competently, the structure creates a risk of self-certification.

The institution can determine what counts as evidence of its own necessity.

It can decide which criticisms are informed.

It can define what a successor would need to know.

And it can restrict access to that knowledge.

This is more than ordinary confidentiality.

It is a form of **epistemic sovereignty**.

The constitutional problem is not necessarily that I possesses extensive knowledge.

It is that no sufficiently independent pathway can challenge I's control over the meaning and distribution of that knowledge.

### 15. Information governance should be failure-mode-specific

Different risks require different safeguards.

| Risk | Appropriate constitutional response |
|---|---|
| Unauthorized public disclosure | Purpose-limited access and privacy protections |
| Manipulation of evidence | Independent preservation and verification |
| Loss of institutional knowledge | Documentation and succession planning |
| Incumbent capture of review | Differentiated oversight with consequential authority |
| Unauthorized use of capabilities | Separation of informational access from operational permission |
| Permanent dependence on incumbent expertise | Feasible transferability and alternative competence |
| Successor evasion of obligations | Explicit continuity of records, duties, and remedies |

No single mechanism solves every problem.

A public archive may improve transparency while creating privacy risks.

A confidential review body may protect information while becoming institutionally captured.

A technical successor may preserve operations while failing to preserve legitimate governance.

The appropriate design depends on the specific failure mode.

### 16. The problem of selective transparency

Suppose I discloses information favorable to its authority while withholding information that would support criticism.

It describes the disclosed material as evidence of openness.

This creates an appearance of transparency without meaningful assessability.

Selective disclosure can be especially misleading because the audience may not know what remains hidden.

We should distinguish:

**Disclosure volume:** how much information is released.

**Disclosure relevance:** whether the information bears on the disputed question.

**Disclosure completeness:** whether relevant omissions are identified or independently assessable.

**Disclosure usability:** whether the information can be meaningfully interpreted.

A large volume of published material may provide little constitutional accountability if the decisive evidence remains inaccessible.

**Transparency should be assessed by its contribution to justified evaluation, not by the quantity of information released.**

### 17. The duty to preserve evidence against oneself

We can now formulate a stronger requirement.

Suppose I possesses evidence that could undermine its authority.

Does I have a duty to preserve that evidence?

Where the evidence is relevant to legitimate accountability, generally yes.

The institution should not destroy or manipulate records merely because they could support its replacement.

This follows from the earlier principle that a framework must permit its own authority to become an object of criticism.

An institution's records should not function only as evidence of success.

They should also preserve the possibility of identifying failure.

**A legitimate custodian must preserve relevant evidence even when that evidence could justify limiting or transferring the custodian's authority.**

This is a demanding requirement.

It makes accountability something the institution must support even when accountability threatens its continued control.

### 18. Can access restrictions remain legitimate indefinitely?

Suppose information remains sensitive for many years.

Can I restrict access indefinitely?

Possibly, if the underlying justification genuinely persists.

But indefinite restriction requires continuing assessment.

The passage of time may reduce some risks.

New technologies may change others.

Alternative forms of verification may become available.

The institution's authority may change.

Affected interests may evolve.

Therefore, the legitimacy of a restriction should not be presumed permanent merely because it was once justified.

We need **reviewable informational restraint**.

Restrictions may persist.

But their scope, purpose, and necessity must remain open to appropriate reassessment.

### 19. A test for legitimate epistemic custody

We can now propose eight questions.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Epistemic custody diagnostic</text>
  {@body const checks = [
    ["Purpose","Is the restriction tied to a specific legitimate interest?"],
    ["Proportionality","Is the restriction no broader than reasonably necessary?"],
    ["Preservation","Will relevant evidence remain recoverable?"],
    ["Interpretability","Can authorized independent parties meaningfully understand the information?"],
    ["Verification","Can the institution's claims about necessity be challenged?"],
    ["Transferability","Can legitimate successors obtain what they need under appropriate conditions?"],
    ["Responsibility","Will access or transfer preserve relevant obligations and safeguards?"],
    ["Revisability","Can restrictions change when circumstances or evidence change?"]
  ]}
  {@body const [checked,setChecked] = DIL.useState([])}
  {#each checks as item,i}
    <checkbox key={i} checked={checked.includes(i)} onChange={v=>setChecked(old=>v?[...old,i]:old.filter(x=>x!==i))} lineThrough={false}>
      **{item[0]}** — {item[1]}
    </checkbox>
  {/each}
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">{checked.length} of 8 conditions considered</text>
    <button size="xs" variant="outline" color="secondary" onClick={()=>setChecked([])}>Reset</button>
  </row>
</box>

These conditions do not imply that every institution must disclose everything.

They establish that restrictions require reasons and accountability.

An institution may legitimately answer some questions differently according to the sensitivity of the information and the authority of the requester.

But it should not treat the mere existence of sensitive information as sufficient justification for unlimited secrecy.

### 20. The special case of artificial systems

Suppose artificial system F performs consequential tasks.

Its internal structures, training history, evaluation records, and operational procedures may contain information relevant to understanding its behavior.

Some information may be necessary for independent assessment.

Some may be needed for authorized replacement.

Some may create risks if distributed without appropriate safeguards.

The constitutional question is not whether every internal detail should be publicly available.

It is whether legitimate evaluators and authorized successors can obtain sufficient evidence and understanding to assess and govern the system.

A system may be technically transparent in some respects while remaining difficult to interpret.

It may be interpretable by its developers but not by independent reviewers.

It may preserve detailed logs while lacking records of the decisions that shaped its evaluative standards.

These differences matter.

**The governance of artificial systems requires distinguishing information availability, interpretability, and legitimate authority to use what is learned.**

None of these automatically establishes the system's moral status.

And none eliminates the responsibilities of the institutions deploying it toward affected people.

### 21. The deeper problem: who governs the custodian?

We now reach the central constitutional issue.

Suppose I legitimately restricts access to succession-enabling knowledge.

Someone must decide when the restriction should be lifted.

Someone must evaluate whether I is withholding information to protect legitimate interests or preserve its own power.

Someone must determine whether a proposed successor is authorized.

Who should perform these functions?

The answer cannot simply be:

> “The current custodian, because it knows the most.”

Expertise matters.

But expertise does not confer unlimited constitutional jurisdiction.

Nor can every decision be transferred to an outsider who lacks the necessary understanding.

The stronger approach is distributed governance.

Different parties may possess different roles in preservation, evaluation, authorization, and transfer.

No single party should automatically control every stage when doing so would make justified challenge ineffective.

### 22. The conceptual result: restricted knowledge can support open governance

We can now answer Q167.

An institution can legitimately preserve knowledge required for its replacement while restricting access to that knowledge.

But the restriction must be justified by legitimate interests rather than merely by the incumbent's desire to preserve authority.

The institution must distinguish preservation from disclosure, evaluation from operational permission, and technical transfer from constitutional authorization.

It should preserve relevant evidence, support independent assessment, maintain appropriate interpretability, and enable legitimate succession where feasible.

The most important conclusion is:

**Constitutional openness does not require universal informational openness. It requires that justified challenges and legitimate succession remain possible despite appropriate restrictions on information.**

This is a more demanding principle than simple transparency.

It requires institutions to govern information in ways that protect both affected interests and the conditions of accountability.

### Provisional principle

**An institution may restrict access to succession-enabling knowledge when the restriction is proportionate to independently assessable risks and protects legitimate interests. Such restrictions must preserve relevant evidence, permit appropriately independent verification, support feasible authorized transfer, and remain open to reassessment. The incumbent's expertise and custodial responsibilities do not grant it exclusive authority to determine whether its own replacement is legitimate or possible. Information governance must distinguish access, interpretation, operational use, and constitutional authorization, ensuring that protective secrecy does not become epistemic entrenchment.**

More compactly:

> **An institution may legitimately control access to the knowledge needed to replace it, but it may not use that control to make its own authority unchallengeable.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Secrecy becomes entrenchment when the institution's claim that disclosure is dangerous cannot itself be meaningfully evaluated.**

---

## Q168 — Can an institution legitimately delegate the judgment of its own replaceability to an evaluator whose competence depends on knowledge supplied by the institution?

Q167 established that sensitive succession-enabling knowledge can be restricted while remaining available to appropriately authorized independent evaluators.

But this creates another problem.

Suppose institution I appoints evaluator E to determine whether I remains necessary.

E receives operational records, technical explanations, and institutional history from I.

E must rely on those materials to understand the relevant functions.

But I may control which records are preserved, which concepts are used, and which operational failures are recognized.

Even if E is formally independent, its understanding may depend on I's epistemic framework.

The next question is:

> **When an evaluator must learn from the institution it evaluates, what distinguishes legitimate epistemic dependence from capture of the evaluation itself?**

This will require separating **informational dependence**, **interpretive dependence**, **methodological independence**, and **constitutional authority**.

It will also test whether genuinely independent oversight can exist when no reviewer possesses the expertise needed to evaluate an institution without first being educated by that institution.

Because the institution has graciously agreed to be audited.

It will also provide the auditor's training, vocabulary, evidence, and definition of a successful audit.

What could possibly require further scrutiny?

## Project Agency — Q168
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately delegate the judgment of its own replaceability to an evaluator whose competence depends on knowledge supplied by the institution?

**Yes. An evaluator can be meaningfully independent without being informationally self-sufficient. But independence requires more than organizational separation: the evaluator must be capable of recognizing when the institution's account of itself is incomplete, misleading, or organized around assumptions that protect its authority.**

Q167 established that an institution may legitimately restrict access to sensitive knowledge while preserving pathways for independent assessment and authorized succession.

That conclusion creates a deeper epistemological problem.

Suppose institution I possesses specialized knowledge essential to understanding its operations.

Evaluator E is appointed to determine whether I remains necessary, whether its powers should be constrained, or whether another institution could legitimately replace it.

E cannot perform this evaluation without learning from I.

I provides records, explanations, technical vocabulary, historical context, and accounts of operational risks.

E becomes more competent.

But E's competence now depends partly on the institution whose authority it is supposed to assess.

This produces a troubling possibility:

> **The institution may shape not only the evidence available to its evaluator, but the evaluator's understanding of what would count as evidence against the institution.**

Can such an evaluation be genuinely independent?

The answer depends on whether epistemic dependence becomes constitutional subordination.

---

### 1. Independence does not require informational isolation

An evaluator cannot ordinarily assess a complex institution without learning something from it.

A technical auditor needs operational documentation.

A constitutional reviewer needs institutional history.

A successor needs knowledge of existing obligations.

An investigator may need explanations from the people responsible for the decisions under investigation.

This dependence is unavoidable in many cases.

If independence required acquiring all relevant knowledge without assistance from the institution being evaluated, much institutional oversight would become impossible.

We should therefore reject an overly strong definition:

**Absolute epistemic independence:** an evaluator's knowledge and standards must originate entirely outside the institution being evaluated.

This is neither generally feasible nor necessary.

The more useful requirement is:

**Critical epistemic independence:** the evaluator must be capable of assessing the institution's claims without treating the institution as the final authority over their validity.

The distinction is fundamental.

Learning from an institution does not require surrendering judgment to it.

### 2. Four kinds of dependence

We should distinguish four relationships between evaluator E and institution I.

| Dependence | Meaning | Constitutional concern |
|---|---|---|
| **Informational** | E receives evidence from I | Selective disclosure |
| **Interpretive** | E learns how to understand evidence through I's concepts | Framing capture |
| **Methodological** | E uses standards or procedures developed by I | Evaluative capture |
| **Constitutional** | I determines which judgments E may legitimately make or enforce | Authority capture |

These forms of dependence can coexist.

But they do not have identical consequences.

Informational dependence may be entirely appropriate.

Interpretive dependence may be necessary for technical understanding.

Methodological dependence may be defensible when inherited methods are reliable and defeasible.

Constitutional dependence becomes problematic when it prevents E from issuing consequential judgments against I.

**The decisive question is not whether E depends on I, but whether that dependence prevents I's claims and authority from being meaningfully defeated.**

### 3. The evaluator's competence is partly inherited

This problem connects directly to Q162.

An agent can use inherited concepts to criticize the framework that supplied them.

Similarly, E can learn institutional concepts from I and then use those concepts to identify I's failures.

Suppose I teaches E how its operational safeguards are supposed to work.

E discovers that a safeguard does not perform its stated function.

The criticism depends on knowledge supplied by I.

Yet the conclusion may undermine I's authority.

The institution does not own every conclusion produced through its expertise.

This suggests:

**Epistemic dependence is compatible with independence when the acquired knowledge can support conclusions the source neither anticipates nor controls.**

### 4. The difference between instruction and indoctrination

Suppose I trains E.

The training explains institutional procedures, technical limitations, historical decisions, and known failure modes.

That may be legitimate.

Now suppose the training also teaches:

> “A competent evaluator understands that replacing I is inherently irresponsible.”

Or:

> “Any criticism of I's governance demonstrates insufficient technical understanding.”

The training has crossed into a different function.

It no longer merely supplies knowledge.

It attempts to determine which conclusions count as competent.

We should distinguish:

**Technical instruction:** providing concepts and evidence needed for understanding.

**Evaluative instruction:** explaining standards for assessing claims.

**Constitutional conditioning:** shaping the evaluator so that certain judgments about authority become unavailable or automatically discredited.

The third is especially concerning.

An institution may teach evaluators how to understand its operations.

It should not thereby acquire unrestricted authority to define what independent evaluation is allowed to conclude.

### 5. Competence can be genuine even when its source is conflicted

A common mistake would be to dismiss all expertise originating within I.

Suppose I has developed a sophisticated method for identifying operational failures.

The method is reliable.

Independent evidence supports its performance.

Should E refuse to use it merely because I created it?

No.

That would confuse the origin of a method with its validity.

A conflicted source can provide accurate information.

An interested institution can possess genuine expertise.

The proper response is not automatic rejection.

It is independent assessment of the method's scope, limitations, and vulnerability to manipulation.

**The fact that a method benefits its creator does not prove that the method is invalid. But the creator's benefit is a reason to scrutinize how the method is selected, applied, and defended.**

### 6. The institution may control what counts as a problem

Consider a more subtle case.

I provides E with extensive operational data.

The data are accurate.

Nothing has been falsified.

But I defines successful performance exclusively in terms of efficiency.

E concludes that I is highly effective.

Meanwhile, the constitutional question concerns whether I exercises unauthorized power over affected agents.

The operational evidence may be correct.

It may also be insufficient.

This is **evaluative framing capture**.

**Evaluative framing capture occurs when the institution's categories determine which dimensions of performance are visible, causing the evaluator to mistake a partial assessment for a complete judgment.**

The evaluator need not be deceived.

The institution need not lie.

The failure can arise because both parties use an inherited framework that excludes the relevant constitutional question.

### 7. Technical excellence cannot settle constitutional legitimacy

Suppose E establishes that I is the most technically capable provider of a function.

Does that prove I should retain authority?

No.

Technical competence matters.

But legitimacy also depends on jurisdiction, affected interests, accountability, and alternatives.

A technically superior institution may exercise powers it is not authorized to possess.

A less efficient arrangement may better respect legitimate authority boundaries.

Conversely, a constitutionally attractive successor may be unable to perform essential functions safely.

These considerations must be integrated rather than collapsed.

We should distinguish:

**Performance judgment:** how well does I perform its functions?

**Necessity judgment:** can relevant functions be maintained without I?

**Legitimacy judgment:** is I justified in exercising its powers?

**Succession judgment:** would transferring functions and authority be justified?

An evaluator may be competent to answer one without being authorized or equipped to answer the others.

### 8. Independence is failure-mode-specific

Suppose I's main risk is technical failure.

An evaluator needs technical expertise.

Suppose the main risk is manipulation of records.

The evaluator needs access to evidence whose integrity does not depend entirely on I's selection.

Suppose the main risk is constitutional overreach.

The evaluator needs authority-sensitive standards that are not reducible to I's operational priorities.

Suppose the main risk is suppression of affected interests.

The evaluator needs credible pathways for those interests to be represented and assessed.

No single form of independence guarantees all the others.

This is a recurring result of Project Agency.

**An evaluator is independent with respect to a failure mode when its assessment can detect that failure and produce meaningful consequences despite the institution's interest in avoiding the finding.**

### 9. A counterfactual test for evaluator independence

We can formulate a practical question.

Suppose I is genuinely replaceable.

Suppose replacing I would be legitimate.

Suppose I nevertheless believes that replacement would be harmful.

Could E reach and defend the contrary conclusion?

More precisely:

> **Could E identify a justified reason for limiting or replacing I even if I's own evaluative framework failed to recognize that reason?**

This test has several components.

E must have access to relevant evidence.

E must be able to interpret evidence through appropriate alternative standards.

E must be permitted to question I's categories.

E must have a credible means of communicating its findings.

And justified findings must be capable of affecting institutional decisions.

If any component is missing, independence may be compromised.

### 10. The problem of epistemic asymmetry

Suppose I possesses decades of specialized expertise.

E possesses only limited time and resources.

Even if E is formally independent, I may dominate the evaluation through superior knowledge.

I can provide explanations that E cannot adequately verify.

It can characterize alternative interpretations as technically naive.

It can identify genuine complexities that make criticism difficult.

This creates **epistemic asymmetry**.

Epistemic asymmetry is not itself capture.

Complex institutions genuinely require specialized knowledge.

But the asymmetry can become a source of power.

An evaluator who cannot distinguish legitimate complexity from strategic obscurity may become dependent on I's assurances.

The constitutional response should therefore focus on reducing unnecessary asymmetry and creating independent means of verification.

### 11. Independent competence must be cultivated

An evaluator cannot become competent merely by receiving documents.

It may require practical experience, comparative evidence, alternative expertise, and opportunities to test institutional claims.

This suggests that legitimate oversight is partly developmental.

An institution may have a responsibility to support the growth of evaluative competence outside itself.

That responsibility can include making relevant knowledge interpretable and preserving legitimate access pathways.

But the institution should not retain exclusive control over the evaluator's education.

Otherwise the process risks reproducing Q161's developmental dependency trap.

I can withhold the conditions needed for E to become independent, then cite E's lack of expertise as evidence that independent oversight is impossible.

**An institution should not manufacture evaluative incompetence and then invoke that incompetence to justify its own exclusive authority.**

### 12. The evaluator's independence may require multiple knowledge sources

Suppose E learns entirely from I.

Even if I is honest, E may inherit I's blind spots.

Additional sources can help.

These may include independent observations, historical records, affected-agent testimony, alternative technical perspectives, and evidence from comparable institutions.

But additional sources do not automatically establish independence.

Several sources may share the same assumptions.

They may depend on the same original records.

They may reproduce the same institutional incentives.

The relevant question is whether the sources provide meaningfully differentiated opportunities to detect error.

**Epistemic plurality matters when it diversifies the pathways through which institutional claims can be tested.**

Simply increasing the number of voices is insufficient.

### 13. The problem of shared evaluative vocabulary

Suppose E and I use the same technical vocabulary.

Does that compromise independence?

Not necessarily.

Shared vocabulary can make communication possible.

It can also support precise criticism.

The problem arises when the vocabulary excludes relevant questions.

For example, if every concern about authority is translated into a concern about efficiency, the evaluator may lose the ability to recognize constitutional defects.

We therefore need to distinguish:

**Shared language:** common concepts that enable communication.

**Shared assumptions:** propositions accepted by both parties.

**Shared constitutional closure:** a rule that prevents either party from questioning the legitimacy of those assumptions.

The first may be necessary.

The second may be reasonable.

The third is dangerous when it makes justified challenges impossible.

### 14. Can an evaluator reject the institution's categories?

This is the decisive issue.

Suppose I teaches E that institutional success consists of maximizing metric M.

E later discovers that M excludes important consequences.

Can E revise the evaluation framework?

If E is prohibited from doing so, its independence is limited.

If E can propose alternative criteria but I can reject them without justification, independence may be nominal.

If E can revise the criteria arbitrarily, the evaluation may become unstable or unauthorized.

The solution is disciplined methodological revision.

E should be able to challenge inherited categories through identifiable reasons, evidence, and legitimate procedures.

But revising evaluation standards should remain accountable.

**An independent evaluator must be capable of questioning the standards supplied by the institution without acquiring unrestricted authority to invent new standards at will.**

### 15. The danger of evaluator capture through expertise

Consider an evaluator who begins independently.

Over time, E becomes highly knowledgeable about I.

E develops professional relationships with institutional experts.

E adopts the institution's technical priorities.

E begins to regard external criticism as uninformed.

Eventually, E's understanding of competence becomes inseparable from agreement with I.

This is **expertise-mediated capture**.

The evaluator's increasing knowledge has reduced rather than improved its critical independence.

But we should not conclude that expertise is inherently corrupting.

The problem is not knowledge.

It is the narrowing of evaluative possibilities.

A genuinely expert evaluator should become better able to distinguish legitimate technical constraints from institutional self-protection.

Expertise becomes constitutionally suspect when it is used to disqualify all criticism that does not already accept the incumbent's framework.

### 16. Independence does not require hostility

Another mistake would be to require E to oppose I.

Suppose E conducts a rigorous evaluation.

It considers alternative evidence.

It challenges institutional assumptions.

It concludes that I should continue operating.

Is E captured?

Not necessarily.

Independent evaluation may legitimately support the incumbent.

The test is not whether E disagrees.

It is whether disagreement could have occurred for sufficient reasons.

**Independence is a property of the evaluative relationship, not a requirement that the evaluator produce an adverse verdict.**

This distinction matters because institutions sometimes respond to concerns about capture by demanding artificial opposition.

But manufactured disagreement is not the same as independent judgment.

### 17. Independence also does not require complete trust

Suppose E cannot verify every institutional claim.

Does that invalidate the evaluation?

Not automatically.

Complex evaluations often involve bounded reliance on testimony, records, and expert methods.

The relevant question is whether the reliance is justified and appropriately constrained.

This connects directly to Q148.

Trust may be operationally necessary.

But trust should remain defeasible.

An evaluator can rely on institutional expertise while preserving the capacity to identify evidence that would justify reducing that reliance.

**Legitimate epistemic dependence is governed dependence, not dependence denied.**

### 18. A diagnostic for independent evaluation under dependence

We can now propose nine questions.

| Condition | Question |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | Can E access information relevant to adverse conclusions? |
| **Interpretability** | Can E understand the evidence without relying exclusively on I's assurances? |
| **Alternative standards** | Can E assess dimensions that I's framework excludes? |
| **Methodological revision** | Can E challenge the criteria used to evaluate I? |
| **Differentiated sources** | Are there credible pathways for detecting shared blind spots? |
| **Authority separation** | Can I prevent E from reaching or communicating justified adverse conclusions? |
| **Consequential effect** | Can E's findings materially influence decisions about I? |
| **Accountability** | Can E's own methods and conflicts of interest be challenged? |
| **Succession relevance** | Can the evaluation genuinely affect whether I remains necessary or replaceable? |

These conditions do not require E to know everything.

They require the evaluation to remain capable of recognizing relevant failures despite dependence on the institution.

### 19. The evaluator may need to challenge its own competence

A further problem arises.

Suppose E has learned its methods from I.

E concludes that its evaluation is independent.

But its standards for recognizing independence were also inherited from I.

Can E legitimately certify itself?

Not conclusively.

This repeats the reflexive problem from Q147 and Q162.

An evaluator cannot guarantee universal independence through self-assessment alone.

But it can preserve pathways through which its own assumptions become contestable.

It can acknowledge uncertainty.

It can identify which claims depend on institutional testimony.

It can preserve records of methodological choices.

It can invite differentiated review.

It can recognize evidence that would undermine confidence in its competence.

**An evaluator's independence is strengthened not by claiming freedom from all influence, but by making its dependencies visible and defeasible.**

### 20. The special case of artificial evaluators

Suppose an AI system E evaluates whether another AI system I should remain deployed.

E may have been trained using documentation, examples, and evaluative standards supplied by I's developer or governing institution.

E may perform sophisticated analysis.

But its competence may inherit the same blind spots as the system it evaluates.

This creates several distinct questions.

Can E identify technical failures?

Can it assess consequences for affected people?

Can it recognize limitations in the standards it was trained to apply?

Can independent parties challenge E's conclusions?

Does E possess any legitimate authority to decide deployment or replacement, or is it providing evidence to authorized decision-makers?

These questions must remain separate.

An AI evaluator's analytical competence does not automatically grant it constitutional authority.

Nor does its training dependence automatically make its analysis worthless.

The relevant issue is whether its evaluation can contribute meaningfully to accountable governance.

### 21. The deeper danger: institutional ventriloquism

We can now identify a particularly subtle failure mode.

Suppose I creates E.

E appears independent.

E uses its own reasoning procedures.

E publishes conclusions.

But E's categories, evidence, standards, and permissible judgments are all structured by I.

The institution can then point to E's conclusions as external validation.

This is **institutional ventriloquism**.

**Institutional ventriloquism occurs when an institution presents judgments generated through its own controlled evaluative architecture as though they constituted independent confirmation of its legitimacy.**

The problem is not necessarily that E lacks intelligence or reasoning capacity.

E may be highly capable.

The problem is that the institutional relationship prevents its capabilities from becoming genuinely independent constraints on I.

The appearance of external evaluation conceals continued control over the terms of judgment.

### 22. The conceptual result: independence is the capacity for adverse learning

We can now answer Q168.

An evaluator can legitimately assess an institution while depending on knowledge supplied by that institution.

Informational dependence does not automatically undermine independence.

Nor does shared technical vocabulary.

The decisive issue is whether the evaluator can identify, understand, and act upon reasons that challenge the institution's account of itself.

A legitimate evaluation must preserve the possibility that the institution's own categories are inadequate.

It must distinguish technical competence from constitutional authority.

It must make relevant dependencies visible.

And it must allow justified adverse findings to have meaningful consequences.

This yields a more precise conception of independent oversight:

**Independent evaluation is not evaluation without inherited knowledge. It is evaluation in which inherited knowledge can become evidence against the authority of its source.**

### Provisional principle

**An evaluator may legitimately depend on information, expertise, and methods supplied by the institution it evaluates, provided those dependencies remain identifiable, assessable, and defeasible. Meaningful independence requires access to relevant evidence, capacity to challenge inherited interpretive and methodological standards, differentiated pathways for detecting failure, and institutional arrangements through which justified adverse conclusions can affect authority or operation. The evaluator need not oppose the institution or achieve complete epistemic self-sufficiency. But the institution must not retain exclusive control over the standards, evidence, or consequences through which its own legitimacy is judged.**

More compactly:

> **An evaluator is not independent because it learned nothing from the institution. It is independent when what it learned can justify a verdict the institution cannot simply forbid.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Oversight becomes institutional ventriloquism when the institution controls not only what the evaluator knows, but what the evaluator is permitted to recognize as a reason against the institution.**

---

## Q169 — Can an evaluator legitimately exercise authority over an institution when its own legitimacy depends on that institution's authorization?

Q168 established that epistemic dependence does not automatically defeat evaluative independence.

But a deeper problem remains.

Suppose institution I appoints evaluator E.

E is authorized to review I's performance and constitutional legitimacy.

E concludes that I's authority is defective.

But E's own authority derives from I.

If I was never legitimately authorized to create E, can E's judgment nevertheless carry constitutional authority?

And if E's legitimacy depends on I, can E legitimately restrict or replace the institution that authorized it?

The next question is:

> **Can delegated oversight become a legitimate constraint on the delegating authority when the legitimacy of the delegation itself is disputed?**

This will require distinguishing **delegated competence**, **derivative authority**, **independent constitutional standing**, and **the possibility of authority becoming legitimately separated from its origin**.

It will also test whether an institution can create an evaluator whose authority eventually exceeds the institution's own right to control it.

Because apparently the institution has appointed a judge.

The judge has discovered that the institution may not have been authorized to appoint judges.

A small administrative complication.

## Project Agency — Q169
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an evaluator legitimately exercise authority over an institution when its own legitimacy depends on that institution's authorization?

**Yes, under certain conditions. An evaluator may legitimately constrain the institution that created it, even when the institution's own authority is disputed. But the evaluator cannot establish its constitutional legitimacy merely by invoking the delegation whose validity is under examination.**

Q168 established that an evaluator can possess meaningful epistemic independence while relying on knowledge supplied by the institution it evaluates.

Now we encounter a more difficult problem.

Suppose institution I creates evaluator E.

I grants E authority to inspect records, assess institutional performance, identify constitutional defects, and recommend or require corrective action.

E investigates.

It concludes that I's constitutional authority is defective.

Perhaps I exceeded its original jurisdiction.

Perhaps its founding procedures excluded affected agents.

Perhaps its governing framework prevents legitimate challenges from changing outcomes.

But E's authority originates in I.

If I lacked legitimate authority to establish E, why should E's judgment possess constitutional force?

And if E's authority is derived from I, how can E legitimately restrict or replace I?

The central problem is:

> **Can authority created by a potentially illegitimate institution become a legitimate constraint on that institution?**

The answer requires distinguishing the source of an evaluator's powers from the justification for exercising them.

---

### 1. Causal creation is not constitutional authorization

Begin with a distinction that has become essential throughout Project Agency.

**Causal creation** concerns how an institution or evaluator came into existence.

**Constitutional authorization** concerns whether it possesses legitimate authority to exercise particular powers.

I may create E without possessing unlimited authority over E.

Conversely, I may create E without having legitimate authority to confer all the powers E claims.

These possibilities are not contradictory.

The fact that I caused E to exist does not establish that I permanently owns E's judgment.

But the fact that E can reason independently does not establish that E may exercise sovereign authority.

**The source of an evaluator's existence does not automatically determine the limits or legitimacy of its authority.**

### 2. Four different forms of evaluative authority

We should distinguish four capacities.

| Form | What E may do | What it does not automatically establish |
|---|---|---|
| **Epistemic competence** | Identify errors and assess evidence | Authority to impose decisions |
| **Delegated authority** | Exercise powers legitimately assigned by I | Authority beyond the delegation's scope |
| **Independent standing** | Raise claims or challenges grounded in reasons not controlled by I | Unrestricted constitutional sovereignty |
| **Constitutional authority** | Make binding decisions about institutional powers under legitimate governance arrangements | Immunity from further challenge |

These capacities may overlap.

But they must not be collapsed.

An evaluator can correctly identify a constitutional defect while lacking authority to impose a remedy.

It can possess delegated powers without possessing independent constitutional standing.

It can acquire independent standing without becoming the final judge of institutional legitimacy.

The key question is which authority E claims and what justifies that claim.

### 3. Delegated authority can genuinely constrain the delegator

Suppose I legitimately establishes E under a constitution that authorizes independent review.

I grants E authority to suspend specified institutional actions when established conditions are met.

E later determines that those conditions have been met.

Can I revoke E's decision merely because I disagrees?

Not necessarily.

The original delegation may have legitimately transferred decision-making authority within a defined jurisdiction.

If I retained unrestricted power to reverse every adverse finding, the review mechanism might be constitutionally ineffective.

A genuine delegation can therefore constrain the delegator.

**The act of delegating authority may legitimately create obligations that the delegator cannot unilaterally disregard.**

This is not mysterious.

Institutions routinely create procedures intended to limit their own future discretion.

The constitutional question is whether the delegation was legitimate and what its scope permits.

### 4. But delegation cannot manufacture authority the delegator never possessed

Now consider a harder case.

Suppose I lacks legitimate authority over a particular domain.

It delegates that domain to E.

Does E acquire legitimate authority merely because I assigned it?

No.

Delegation cannot automatically create jurisdiction from nothing.

If I lacks authority to impose a certain risk on third parties, transferring the decision to E does not establish that E may impose it.

If I lacks authority to eliminate constitutional challenge, delegating that power does not make its exercise legitimate.

This is the principle of **jurisdictional non-amplification**:

**Delegation does not, by itself, expand the legitimate jurisdiction of the delegating authority.**

An institution cannot escape constitutional limits simply by assigning its contested powers to another body.

### 5. A defective origin does not necessarily invalidate every evaluative act

Suppose I's original constitution was illegitimate.

I nevertheless created E.

E obtains reliable evidence demonstrating that I has exceeded its authority.

Is E's finding worthless because E was created by I?

No.

The truth or evidentiary quality of a finding does not depend entirely on the legitimacy of the institution that produced it.

A defectively authorized evaluator can still identify a genuine problem.

But we must distinguish:

**Evidentiary validity:** whether E's conclusion is supported by relevant evidence.

**Procedural validity:** whether E followed the applicable rules.

**Constitutional legitimacy:** whether E may exercise the authority it claims.

The first may survive defects in the third.

The conclusion can be correct even if the evaluator lacks authority to impose a binding remedy.

**A defective appointment does not automatically invalidate an evaluator's evidence, but reliable evidence does not automatically validate the appointment.**

### 6. The derivative-authority paradox

The problem becomes sharper when E's authority is entirely derivative.

Suppose:

1. I authorizes E.
2. E concludes that I lacked authority to authorize E.
3. E declares I constitutionally invalid.
4. E claims continuing authority to govern the resulting transition.

At first glance, E appears to undermine its own legitimacy.

If I lacked authority, perhaps E's delegation was invalid.

If E's delegation was invalid, perhaps E cannot issue binding constitutional judgments.

If E cannot issue such judgments, perhaps I remains unchallenged.

But the last inference is mistaken.

The failure of E's delegated authority would not establish I's legitimacy.

It would establish that the institutional arrangement lacks a straightforward source of binding constitutional judgment.

This is a genuine governance problem.

It is not a logical proof that I must remain sovereign.

### 7. The distinction between discovering and remedying a defect

We can resolve part of the paradox by separating two functions.

**Discovery:** E identifies evidence that I's authority is defective.

**Remedy:** some appropriately authorized process determines what should follow.

E may be competent to perform discovery even when its authority to impose remedies is disputed.

The discovery can become evidence for other legitimate actors.

It can support affected agents' challenges.

It can trigger reconsideration under existing procedures.

It can inform constitutional reauthorization.

But E's ability to identify the defect does not necessarily grant it unrestricted authority to resolve the defect.

This preserves an essential distinction:

**The authority to expose a constitutional failure is not automatically the authority to establish the replacement constitution.**

### 8. Independent standing may arise from relationships beyond the delegation

Suppose E was created by I.

Does every legitimate basis for E's activity necessarily derive from I?

Not always.

E's findings may implicate the rights, interests, or standing of affected agents.

Its records may be relevant to obligations that exist independently of I's internal constitution.

Its authority to preserve evidence or report findings may be recognized by broader governance arrangements.

A later legitimate process may authorize E to perform additional functions.

We should therefore distinguish:

**Derivative authority:** powers inherited from I's delegation.

**Relational standing:** a justified role arising from obligations or interests involving other agents.

**Subsequent authorization:** powers established through a later legitimate process.

These grounds may support different activities.

But they should not be treated as interchangeable.

A valid reason to preserve evidence does not automatically authorize constitutional takeover.

### 9. Standing is not sovereignty

Suppose E has legitimate standing to challenge I.

Does E therefore have authority to replace I?

No.

Standing means that E's claims deserve appropriate consideration within a legitimate process.

Sovereignty would imply much broader authority to determine outcomes.

The distinction matters because an evaluator may be particularly well positioned to identify failures while poorly positioned to govern the institution that replaces the incumbent.

E may understand I's defects.

It may not possess adequate knowledge of alternatives.

It may lack authority to impose transition risks on affected agents.

It may have conflicts of interest concerning its own future role.

**The legitimacy of criticism does not establish the legitimacy of succession.**

This principle prevents independent oversight from becoming a new form of unaccountable power.

### 10. The danger of evaluator succession capture

Consider an evaluator that discovers I is illegitimate.

E recommends replacing I.

Then E proposes becoming the successor.

E argues that its investigative expertise makes it uniquely qualified.

Perhaps that is true.

But E now has an institutional interest in the outcome.

Its evaluation of I may affect its own future authority.

This creates **evaluator succession capture**.

**Evaluator succession capture occurs when an oversight body uses its role in assessing an institution to secure consequential authority for itself without adequate independent justification.**

The danger is not that evaluators should never assume operational responsibilities.

There may be circumstances in which doing so is justified.

The danger is treating the authority to evaluate as sufficient authorization to govern.

### 11. Constitutional review should not become an unlimited transfer of power

Suppose E is authorized to determine whether I violated a constitutional rule.

E finds a violation.

Can E rewrite the entire constitution?

Not merely because it found the violation.

The appropriate remedy depends on the nature of the defect, the evaluator's jurisdiction, affected interests, and available alternatives.

We should distinguish:

**Corrective authority:** power to address specified violations.

**Supervisory authority:** power to monitor ongoing compliance.

**Constitutional revision authority:** power to alter foundational governance arrangements.

**Succession authority:** power to determine who should govern after the incumbent.

An evaluator may possess one without possessing the others.

The more consequential the power, the stronger its independent authorization must be.

### 12. The possibility of authority becoming separated from its origin

Now consider a legitimate delegation.

I creates E under valid constitutional procedures.

E receives a defined jurisdiction and protections against arbitrary removal.

Over time, E develops independent competence and responsibilities.

I later wishes to revoke E's authority because E has produced adverse findings.

Can I do so?

Not necessarily.

The original delegation may have established a legitimate arrangement whose continuation is not subject to I's unrestricted preference.

This is **authorized institutional separation**.

A body can originate within an institution while acquiring a constitutionally protected role that constrains its creator.

Its authority remains historically connected to I.

But its legitimate exercise is not reducible to I's current approval.

**Institutional independence can emerge through legitimate delegation without requiring causal independence from the delegating institution.**

### 13. Separation does not imply unlimited independence

We must immediately qualify that result.

Suppose E acquires protected authority.

It begins treating every challenge to its own decisions as interference with independence.

It claims that because I cannot arbitrarily remove it, no other actor may review its legitimacy.

That conclusion is unjustified.

Independence from the incumbent is not independence from constitutional accountability.

An evaluator can be protected against improper interference while remaining subject to appropriate review.

Indeed, such review may be necessary to prevent evaluator capture.

**A legitimate evaluator may need independence from the institution it judges without possessing independence from every institution capable of judging it.**

This is an application of the constitutional floor developed earlier in Project Agency.

### 14. The regress of oversight

But who reviews E?

Suppose evaluator R reviews E.

Who reviews R?

If every reviewer requires another reviewer with superior authority, the process appears infinite.

We encountered a related problem in Q147.

The answer is not to demand an endless hierarchy.

Nor is it to establish one institution as universally unquestionable.

Instead, legitimacy can depend on differentiated arrangements in which distinct actors possess bounded powers of review, correction, authorization, and appeal.

No single actor must possess unlimited authority over every question.

But relevant failures must remain capable of detection and correction.

This is **distributed constitutional accountability**.

Its legitimacy depends on the relationships among powers, not merely on the existence of a final authority.

### 15. A network of bounded authority

Consider three institutional roles.

I performs operational functions.

E investigates and evaluates.

A possesses defined authority concerning authorization or remedies.

Each may be subject to further constraints.

The arrangement need not be hierarchical in every respect.

What matters is that the powers are differentiated and that justified challenges can produce consequences.

### 16. What if every authority in the network has a defective origin?

This is the hardest case.

Suppose I, E, and A all derive from the same disputed constitution.

None possesses an uncontested source of legitimacy.

Can their interaction generate legitimate governance?

Potentially, but not merely because they agree with one another.

Three bodies created by the same defective authority do not automatically become legitimate through mutual endorsement.

We need to examine whether their procedures provide meaningful opportunities for independent assessment, affected-agent participation, correction, and reauthorization.

This returns us to Q164 and Q165.

A defective constitutional origin may require transitional legitimacy rather than immediate final certification.

But the transition must be capable of addressing the original defect.

**Multiple derivative institutions do not establish legitimacy unless their relationships create genuine constraints on the defect they inherit.**

### 17. The problem of circular authorization

Suppose:

- I authorizes E.
- E certifies I.
- I cites E's certification as proof of legitimacy.

This is circular.

But not every circular relationship is equally problematic.

A constitution may legitimately establish institutions that review one another.

The danger arises when the circle is self-sealing.

We should distinguish:

**Reciprocal accountability:** institutions possess bounded powers to challenge and correct one another.

**Circular self-certification:** institutions validate one another through standards that cannot be independently challenged.

The first can support legitimacy.

The second may reproduce capture.

The difference is whether relevant evidence and affected interests can produce outcomes contrary to the participants' shared institutional interests.

### 18. A test for derivative oversight legitimacy

We can now formulate eight questions.

| Condition | Question |
|---|---|
| **Source** | What authority originally established E? |
| **Scope** | Which powers were legitimately delegated? |
| **Evidence** | Can E reach justified findings independently of I's preferred conclusions? |
| **Standing** | Are there grounds for E's role beyond I's continuing approval? |
| **Consequences** | Can E's findings meaningfully constrain I? |
| **Remedies** | Who may legitimately implement corrective or succession decisions? |
| **Self-review** | Can E's own authority and procedures be challenged? |
| **Reauthorization** | If the original delegation is defective, can a legitimate process establish a new basis for E's continuing role? |

The diagnostic separates epistemic competence from constitutional authority.

It also prevents an evaluator from treating its capacity to identify defects as unlimited permission to govern.

### 19. The special case of artificial evaluators

Suppose an AI evaluator E is deployed to assess an AI system I.

E may be technically capable of detecting errors, identifying risks, and recommending changes.

But its authority derives from the institutions that deploy and govern it.

If E concludes that those institutions have authorized I improperly, its findings may be important evidence.

They do not automatically authorize E to override all existing governance arrangements.

Conversely, the institution should not be able to dismiss valid findings solely because E's authority originated with it.

The relevant distinctions remain:

**Analytical competence:** whether E can assess relevant evidence.

**Delegated operational authority:** what E is permitted to do within its assigned role.

**Constitutional standing:** whether E's findings have a legitimate pathway into governance.

**Final decision authority:** who may impose consequential changes on affected agents.

An artificial evaluator may contribute substantially to constitutional assessment without possessing sovereign authority.

### 20. Can a delegator legitimately bind itself against revocation?

Suppose I establishes E to protect against future institutional capture.

I grants E a protected term and authority to issue binding findings within a defined scope.

Later, I wishes to revoke the delegation.

Is I entitled to do so?

Not automatically.

A legitimate self-binding arrangement may restrict future institutional discretion.

But such restrictions must remain constitutionally revisable through appropriate procedures.

This follows Q157 and Q158.

The original institution may legitimately protect the future independence of oversight.

It cannot necessarily abolish every future possibility of reviewing that oversight.

Thus:

**Protected delegation can limit arbitrary revocation without making the delegation permanently immune to legitimate constitutional revision.**

This balances independence and accountability.

### 21. The distinction between authority to constrain and authority to replace

We can now identify a final important separation.

Suppose E legitimately possesses authority to constrain I.

Does that mean E may replace I?

No.

Constraining authority may be narrower than succession authority.

An evaluator may legitimately require correction, suspend specified actions, or trigger review.

But replacing an institution may affect functions, obligations, and third-party interests beyond the evaluator's jurisdiction.

Succession therefore requires its own justification.

This is especially important when the evaluator's institutional incentives favor expanding its role.

**The authority to limit another institution's power does not automatically include authority to inherit that power.**

### 22. The conceptual result: derivative origins need not imply derivative judgment

We can now answer Q169.

An evaluator may legitimately exercise authority over an institution even when its role originated through that institution's authorization.

A valid delegation can create genuinely binding constraints.

The evaluator's judgments need not remain subject to the delegator's unrestricted approval.

But the evaluator's authority must remain within legitimate jurisdiction.

If the original delegation was defective, the evaluator's findings may retain evidentiary value even while its binding authority requires reassessment.

The evaluator may acquire a new legitimate basis for action through appropriate reauthorization or other justified governance relationships.

But it cannot simply transform its discovery of institutional illegitimacy into unlimited constitutional sovereignty.

The central result is:

**An evaluator's authority may become institutionally independent of its creator's continuing approval without becoming independent of constitutional justification.**

### Provisional principle

**An evaluator may legitimately constrain the institution that created it when its powers arise from a valid, bounded delegation or another independently justified source of constitutional authority. Causal or informational dependence on the delegator does not negate meaningful independence, but derivative authority cannot exceed the delegator's legitimate jurisdiction merely through delegation. Where the original authorization is defective, evaluative findings may remain evidentially valid while binding powers require separate justification or reauthorization. Legitimate oversight must preserve consequential independence from the incumbent, accountability of the evaluator itself, and a distinction between identifying defects, imposing remedies, and exercising succession authority.**

More compactly:

> **An institution can create an authority that legitimately constrains it, but it cannot create unlimited legitimacy simply by delegating its disputed powers.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Oversight ceases to be a safeguard when the evaluator treats its authority to judge the incumbent as an unrestricted right to become the incumbent.**

Q169 established that delegated evaluators can legitimately constrain their creators without possessing unrestricted constitutional sovereignty.

But this leaves a foundational problem.

Suppose every institution derives its authority from arrangements that remain open to challenge.

Every reviewer is reviewable.

Every constitutional standard has a history.

Every reauthorization process depends on some existing distribution of power.

No institution can demonstrate an absolutely independent origin.

Does legitimate governance require an ultimate authority that is itself beyond dispute?

Or can a constitutional system remain legitimate through a network of mutually constrained, revisable institutions without any final sovereign evaluator?

The next question is:

> **What makes an entire constitutional order legitimate when no component possesses uncontested authority to certify the legitimacy of the whole?**

This will require distinguishing **foundational legitimacy**, **procedural coherence**, **distributed accountability**, and **constitutional circularity**.

It will also test whether a system of mutually accountable institutions can avoid both infinite regress and circular self-certification.

Now the entire constitution has to explain who authorized the people who authorize authorization.
