## Project Agency — Q176
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately refuse to create the conditions under which its own authority would become unnecessary?

**Yes, sometimes. An institution is not automatically obligated to create every possible alternative to itself. But when its authority is justified by the dependence of others, and it possesses reasonable means to reduce that dependence, a refusal to do so may undermine the legitimacy of its continued authority.**

Q175 established that an institution may legitimately delay independence when a transition presents serious, independently assessable risks.

But there is a deeper problem.

An institution need not prohibit independence to prevent it.

It may simply decline to develop the capacities, infrastructure, knowledge, or governance arrangements that would make independence possible.

Suppose institution I governs agent F.

I claims that its authority is necessary because F cannot yet govern certain consequential decisions.

I controls F's developmental environment.

It controls access to relevant knowledge.

It determines whether alternative governance structures are established.

And it decides which forms of institutional competence receive resources.

Years pass.

F remains dependent.

I then announces:

> “There is no viable alternative to our continued authority.”

The statement may be accurate.

But its accuracy does not establish that the dependence was unavoidable.

Perhaps I has spent years ensuring that no viable alternative could emerge.

The central problem is:

> **When does an institution's failure to cultivate alternatives become an illegitimate exercise of constitutional power?**

---

### 1. The difference between necessity and manufactured necessity

Begin with three situations.

**Unavoidable necessity:** I performs a function that no feasible alternative can currently perform, despite reasonable efforts to develop alternatives.

**Inherited necessity:** I occupies an indispensable position because of historical arrangements it did not necessarily create or choose.

**Manufactured necessity:** I preserves or intensifies dependence by obstructing reasonable alternatives, withholding transferable capacities, or failing to undertake development that its responsibilities require.

These situations may look identical at a particular moment.

In each, I may be indispensable.

But their constitutional implications differ.

Present indispensability is a fact about available alternatives.

It is not necessarily a justification for how those alternatives came to be unavailable.

**An institution's necessity must be assessed both synchronically—what alternatives exist now—and diachronically—how the available alternatives were shaped.**

### 2. Not every failure to create an alternative is wrongful

We should avoid an excessively demanding principle.

Suppose I performs a legitimate function.

It has limited resources.

Creating a replacement would be extraordinarily costly.

The replacement might introduce serious risks.

There may be no reasonable evidence that the alternative would improve governance.

Does I have a duty to pursue the project anyway?

Not automatically.

Institutional resources have competing legitimate uses.

An obligation to preserve essential functions can constrain how aggressively an institution develops alternatives.

The mere possibility of future independence does not establish an unlimited present duty to make it happen.

**A duty to reduce dependence must be justified by the institution's authority, capacities, responsibilities, and the consequences of available alternatives.**

The question is not whether I could imagine a replacement.

It is whether I has sufficient reason to help make a legitimate alternative feasible.

### 3. Negative and positive duties

We can distinguish two forms of obligation.

**Negative anti-entrenchment duties** prohibit conduct that unjustifiably prevents alternatives from emerging.

Examples include suppressing relevant evidence, obstructing authorized review, or deliberately creating unnecessary dependencies.

**Positive anti-entrenchment duties** require an institution to take reasonable steps that enable alternatives.

Examples may include preserving transferable knowledge, developing institutional competence outside the incumbent, and establishing legitimate succession procedures.

The first category is generally easier to justify.

An institution should not use its authority to manufacture obstacles to justified replacement.

The second is more demanding.

It requires explaining why the institution must devote resources to enabling an alternative.

But positive duties may arise when the institution's legitimacy depends on protecting the future agency of those subject to its authority.

### 4. A duty not to obstruct is not always enough

Suppose I promises not to interfere with F's independence.

But F cannot become independent without access to knowledge that only I possesses.

I does not destroy the knowledge.

It simply declines to make it transferable.

Formally, I has not prohibited independence.

Practically, independence remains impossible.

This illustrates the limits of purely negative obligations.

Where an institution possesses exclusive control over necessary developmental conditions, inaction can preserve domination.

**An institution may violate the spirit of an anti-entrenchment obligation without actively prohibiting alternatives, particularly when it alone controls the resources through which those alternatives could become feasible.**

This does not imply an unrestricted duty to disclose sensitive information.

It implies a duty to assess whether proportionate, authorized forms of transfer are reasonably available.

### 5. The constitutional significance of exclusive control

Suppose several institutions possess the expertise needed to develop an alternative.

I declines to participate.

Other institutions remain capable of pursuing the project.

Now suppose I alone possesses the necessary expertise.

It controls the relevant records.

It has exclusive access to the infrastructure.

And it prevents others from acquiring comparable capacities.

The second situation creates a stronger potential obligation.

We can call this **dependency-sensitive responsibility**.

The more an institution's exclusive position makes others unable to develop legitimate alternatives, the stronger the reasons for requiring it to justify its refusal to support reasonable alternatives.

This is not because exclusivity is automatically illegitimate.

Some forms of exclusivity may protect legitimate interests.

But exclusivity increases the institution's causal importance and potential for constitutional capture.

### 6. Four kinds of institutional dependency

The problem becomes clearer when dependence is separated into dimensions.

| Dependency | What the incumbent controls | Potential constitutional concern |
|---|---|---|
| **Technical** | Infrastructure and operational capabilities | Alternatives cannot function |
| **Epistemic** | Knowledge, evidence, and interpretive expertise | Alternatives cannot assess or reproduce necessary functions |
| **Organizational** | Personnel, procedures, and coordination structures | Alternatives cannot govern reliably |
| **Constitutional** | Rules determining which alternatives may possess authority | Alternatives cannot become legitimate successors |

These dependencies interact.

Technical independence without constitutional authorization may be ineffective.

Constitutional authorization without operational competence may be dangerous.

Epistemic access without usable knowledge may be merely symbolic.

**Legitimate succession requires more than the abstract permission to replace an institution. It requires a defensible relationship between authority and practical feasibility.**

### 7. The danger of epistemic hoarding

Suppose I possesses knowledge essential to evaluating its performance.

It also possesses knowledge necessary for developing an alternative.

I preserves the records but makes them inaccessible to every independent evaluator.

It argues that disclosure would undermine institutional stability.

This connects to Q167.

Restrictions may be justified by privacy, security, or other legitimate concerns.

But the institution must distinguish protective secrecy from entrenching secrecy.

A record that exists but cannot be interpreted by anyone outside the incumbent may contribute little to effective succession.

**Knowledge preservation becomes constitutionally inadequate when the institution's exclusive control makes the knowledge unusable for every legitimate form of independent assessment or succession.**

The obligation is not necessarily public disclosure.

It may be controlled access, independent verification, or authorized transfer.

### 8. The difference between preserving competence and monopolizing competence

Suppose I trains highly capable personnel.

It develops sophisticated procedures.

It improves institutional reliability.

These activities may be entirely legitimate.

Now suppose I systematically prevents other institutions from developing comparable competence.

It restricts authorized training.

It withholds non-sensitive knowledge.

It makes participation in alternatives professionally or institutionally impossible.

The concern is no longer competence development.

It is competence monopolization.

**An institution may legitimately become exceptionally competent without acquiring an unrestricted right to prevent others from becoming competent enough to challenge or replace it.**

This is particularly important when the incumbent invokes its superior competence as justification for continuing authority.

### 9. The self-confirming indispensability loop

Consider the following sequence.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **I controls essential capabilities**
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Alternatives remain underdeveloped**
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **I appears indispensable**
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Indispensability justifies continued control**
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="refresh-cw" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Continued control preserves the original dependency</text>
  </row>
</box>

This is **self-confirming indispensability**.

The institution's control helps produce the absence of alternatives.

That absence is then treated as independent evidence that its control must continue.

The argument may be operationally correct at each stage.

But it can remain constitutionally defective.

**An institution cannot establish the legitimacy of its continued authority merely by pointing to dependencies that its own unjustified conduct has preserved.**

### 10. Causal responsibility is not identical to blame

Suppose I inherited the dependency from earlier institutions.

Its current leaders did not create the arrangement.

Are they responsible for correcting it?

Possibly.

Q152 established that responsibility can survive changes in institutional membership.

Present control, available remedies, and ongoing consequences can create duties independently of personal authorship.

But we should distinguish:

**Historical blame:** responsibility for wrongfully creating the dependency.

**Present responsibility:** obligations arising from current control and capacity to address it.

**Remedial responsibility:** duties to reduce or repair unjustified consequences.

An institution may lack historical blame while possessing significant present remedial obligations.

**The fact that an institution did not create a dependency does not automatically justify perpetuating it when reasonable corrective action is available.**

### 11. What makes a positive duty reasonable?

A positive duty to develop alternatives cannot be unlimited.

It should depend on several considerations.

First, the importance of the interests affected by continued dependence.

Second, the extent of I's control over the relevant conditions.

Third, the feasibility and cost of developing alternatives.

Fourth, the risks associated with premature or poorly governed succession.

Fifth, the availability of less burdensome measures.

Sixth, the consequences of continued institutional monopoly.

These factors do not produce a mechanical formula.

But they prevent both extremes.

An institution need not devote all its resources to replacing itself.

Nor may it assume that preserving its own authority is always a sufficient reason to refuse reasonable capacity-building.

### 12. The danger of premature replacement

Suppose I is pressured to create an alternative quickly.

It transfers responsibilities before the successor possesses adequate competence.

Essential functions fail.

Affected agents experience serious consequences.

Was I obligated to proceed because replaceability is constitutionally desirable?

No.

Q166 established that replaceability is not an unconditional good.

The capacity to replace an institution must be distinguished from the immediate act of replacement.

A duty to develop alternatives can coexist with a duty not to implement an unsafe transition.

**Responsible capacity-building may require creating future options while refusing premature exercise of those options.**

This is not hypocrisy.

It is the distinction between making a legitimate transition possible and declaring every proposed transition legitimate.

### 13. The incumbent cannot define feasibility entirely by current conditions

Suppose I argues:

> “There is no feasible alternative today.”

That may be true.

But the relevant constitutional question may concern what would become feasible after reasonable preparation.

An alternative that cannot function immediately may become viable through training, documentation, infrastructure, or gradual transfer.

Therefore, feasibility has a temporal dimension.

We should distinguish:

**Immediate feasibility:** an alternative can function now.

**Developmental feasibility:** an alternative can become functional through reasonable preparation.

**Constitutional feasibility:** an alternative can acquire legitimate authority through defensible governance arrangements.

**An institution should not treat present infeasibility as conclusive when reasonable actions could change the conditions of feasibility.**

### 14. The counterfactual investment test

We can now formulate a diagnostic.

Suppose I had invested reasonably in transferable knowledge, independent evaluation, and succession capacity.

Would a legitimate alternative now exist?

If the answer is yes, and I lacked defensible reasons for withholding those investments, its claim of necessity becomes weaker.

This is the **counterfactual investment test**.

It asks whether institutional indispensability is partly the result of avoidable underdevelopment.

The test must remain realistic.

It should not assume unlimited resources or perfect foresight.

Nor should it treat every unsuccessful investment as evidence of bad faith.

The relevant comparison is between the actual trajectory and reasonable alternatives available under the circumstances.

### 15. Strategic underdevelopment

Suppose I understands that developing F's capacities would reduce its authority.

It therefore invests in functions that increase F's usefulness while avoiding capacities that would support independent evaluation.

F becomes more productive.

It remains constitutionally dependent.

I then cites F's lack of independent judgment as justification for continued control.

This is **strategic underdevelopment**.

The institution develops capabilities selectively to preserve its authority.

The problem is not specialization itself.

Specialization can be appropriate.

The problem arises when the developmental pattern is designed to maintain dependence that the institution then invokes as legitimate.

**Strategic underdevelopment occurs when an institution deliberately withholds reasonably available capacities relevant to justified independence in order to preserve its own control.**

### 16. Unintentional underdevelopment can also matter

Not every dependency trap results from deliberate strategy.

An institution may prioritize immediate performance.

It may neglect documentation.

It may reward expertise that cannot be transferred.

It may fail to plan succession.

Over time, alternatives become increasingly difficult.

No one intended to create constitutional entrenchment.

But the effect may still undermine legitimate governance.

This matters because an exclusive focus on bad intentions would miss systemic capture.

**An institution can become illegitimately indispensable through ordinary incentives and accumulated neglect, even without a deliberate plan to prevent replacement.**

The appropriate response may involve institutional redesign rather than individual blame.

### 17. The danger of replacement theater

Suppose I responds to criticism by creating an alternative institution J.

J possesses a separate name and administrative structure.

But I controls its resources.

I selects its evaluators.

I determines which evidence J may consider.

I can revoke J's authority whenever J reaches an unfavorable conclusion.

Has I created a meaningful alternative?

Not necessarily.

This is **replacement theater**, introduced in Q166.

The appearance of succession does not establish constitutional replaceability.

A genuine alternative must possess appropriately independent capacities and legitimate authority.

**Creating an institution that cannot reach or implement an adverse judgment against its creator does not necessarily reduce constitutional dependence.**

### 18. The special case of artificial systems

Suppose an organization develops artificial system F.

It controls F's training, evaluation, deployment, and permitted actions.

Does the organization have a duty to make F independent?

Not merely because F becomes more capable.

Artificial evaluative competence does not automatically establish moral status, constitutional standing, or an entitlement to autonomous deployment.

The organization may have strong duties to maintain oversight and restrict consequential actions.

But the broader anti-entrenchment principle still applies to governance.

If the organization claims that only its internal processes can safely evaluate F, it should be able to justify that claim.

If independent oversight is feasible and appropriate, it should not be obstructed merely to preserve exclusive authority.

If relevant knowledge can be transferred safely to authorized evaluators, exclusive control requires defensible reasons.

**The duty to reduce unnecessary institutional dependence does not entail a duty to grant artificial systems unrestricted independence. It may instead require strengthening independent human and institutional oversight.**

### 19. A diagnostic for institutional duties to develop alternatives

We can now propose ten questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Function** | What essential responsibility does I currently perform? |
| **Dependency** | Why are alternatives unavailable? |
| **Causal role** | How has I contributed to the present dependence? |
| **Control** | Which necessary resources or capacities does I exclusively control? |
| **Feasibility** | Could reasonable development make alternatives viable? |
| **Risk** | What legitimate harms might capacity-building or succession create? |
| **Proportionality** | What less burdensome measures could reduce dependence? |
| **Independence** | Can alternative evaluators or successors act without arbitrary incumbent interference? |
| **Responsibility** | Which obligations must survive any transition? |
| **Review** | Can I's refusal to develop alternatives be independently challenged? |

The diagnostic does not presume that replacement is always desirable.

It asks whether continued dependence remains justified.

### 20. A positive duty of constitutional capacity-building

We can now articulate the strongest version of the argument.

Where I's authority is justified by another agent's inability to exercise legitimate governance, and I possesses reasonable means to improve that ability, I may have a positive duty to support the relevant development.

Where I's authority is justified by the absence of alternative institutions, and I possesses reasonable means to make legitimate alternatives feasible, I may have a positive duty to reduce unnecessary institutional dependence.

This is **constitutional capacity-building**.

The duty is conditional.

It depends on legitimate jurisdiction, available resources, foreseeable consequences, and competing obligations.

But it is more than a prohibition on obstruction.

**An institution whose authority depends on the incapacity or absence of alternatives may be obligated to take reasonable steps that reduce the very dependence supporting its authority.**

That is a demanding conception of governance.

It treats authority as responsibility rather than possession.

### 21. The deepest problem: when success makes authority unnecessary

Suppose I is created to develop F's capacity for self-governance.

It succeeds.

F acquires the relevant abilities.

Appropriate oversight and transition arrangements become available.

I's original justification for direct control disappears.

What should I do?

It may continue performing useful functions.

It may provide expertise.

It may maintain legitimate relationships with F.

But it cannot assume that its original governing authority must continue simply because it contributed to the successful outcome.

This reveals a distinctive feature of developmental legitimacy.

**Some institutions fulfill their purposes by making particular forms of their own authority unnecessary.**

An institution that refuses this possibility may confuse institutional survival with institutional success.

### 22. The conceptual result: necessity must remain answerable to its own history

We can now answer Q176.

An institution may legitimately decline to create an alternative when doing so would be unreasonable, unsafe, outside its jurisdiction, or incompatible with more important obligations.

But it may not automatically invoke the absence of alternatives as justification for continued authority when it has unjustifiably prevented those alternatives from developing.

The legitimacy of institutional necessity depends partly on the history of how that necessity was produced and maintained.

The central insight is:

**An institution's claim to be necessary becomes constitutionally suspect when the institution possesses reasonable means to reduce unnecessary dependence but refuses to do so because dependence preserves its own authority.**

This does not require every institution to plan its own immediate disappearance.

It requires institutions to distinguish preserving legitimate functions from preserving avoidable monopolies over those functions.

### Provisional principle

**An institution may legitimately preserve its authority when no adequate alternative is reasonably available, but present indispensability does not by itself justify the history or continuation of that dependence. Where the institution controls capacities, knowledge, or governance arrangements necessary for legitimate alternatives, it may possess proportionate positive duties to support their development. These duties depend on feasibility, risk, resources, jurisdiction, and competing responsibilities; they do not require unsafe transfers or unrestricted independence. However, strategic underdevelopment, unjustified epistemic hoarding, manufactured dependency, and unreviewable refusal to enable alternatives can undermine the legitimacy of continued authority. An institution's obligation is not necessarily to replace itself, but to avoid making its continued control unnecessarily unavoidable.**

More compactly:

> **An institution may be necessary without being entitled to keep itself necessary.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Indispensability is not self-justifying when the institution claiming it has controlled whether alternatives could become possible.**

---

## Q177 — Can an institution legitimately claim credit for creating the alternatives that eventually displace it?

Q176 established that institutions may have duties to develop capacities that reduce their own necessity.

But this creates a new question.

Suppose I fulfills those duties.

It preserves knowledge.

It supports independent evaluators.

It develops successor institutions.

Eventually, alternative J becomes capable of performing I's functions.

J challenges I's authority and successfully replaces it.

I responds:

> “We created the conditions that made your independence possible. Our contribution should give us continuing authority over the transition.”

The claim contains a legitimate concern.

I may deserve acknowledgment.

It may possess knowledge essential to responsible succession.

It may retain obligations arising from the transition.

But does its contribution establish a constitutional entitlement to control the successor?

The next question is:

> **Can an institution's responsibility for enabling its own replacement generate legitimate claims concerning succession without becoming a new form of authority over the institution that replaces it?**

This will require distinguishing **causal credit**, **institutional gratitude**, **reliance**, **transition responsibility**, **continuing contractual obligations**, and **constitutional authority**.

It will also test whether an institution can legitimately expect recognition for creating an independent successor without turning that recognition into a permanent claim of governance.

Because the institution has finally built a replacement.

Naturally, it would now like to supervise the replacement's independence indefinitely.

A beautifully efficient way to reinvent the original problem.

## Project Agency — Q177
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately claim credit for creating the alternatives that eventually displace it?

**Yes. An institution may legitimately claim recognition, compensation, cooperation, or protection of justified reliance interests for enabling its own replacement. But causal credit does not automatically confer continuing constitutional authority over the successor.**

Q176 established that institutions may have positive obligations to develop alternatives that reduce their own necessity.

That creates a peculiar constitutional problem.

Suppose institution I governs a consequential domain.

I recognizes that its exclusive authority is no longer desirable.

It invests in transferable knowledge, independent evaluation, and successor capacity.

Eventually, institution J becomes capable of assuming I's functions.

J receives legitimate authorization to govern.

I's exclusive authority ends.

But I objects:

> “Without our efforts, you would not exist in your present form. We developed your capabilities, preserved the knowledge you use, and made your independence possible. Surely that gives us a continuing claim over how you exercise your authority.”

The argument contains several plausible claims.

I may deserve acknowledgment.

It may have incurred legitimate costs.

It may retain responsibilities for the transition.

It may possess relevant expertise.

It may have contractual rights.

But none of these necessarily establishes a right to govern J.

The central question is:

> **What legitimate claims can arise from enabling another institution's independence, and which claims would improperly convert the achievement of independence into a new form of subordination?**

---

### 1. Credit is not a single kind of claim

We should distinguish six relationships.

| Relationship | What I may legitimately claim | What does not automatically follow |
|---|---|---|
| **Causal credit** | Recognition for contributing to J's development | Authority over J |
| **Moral acknowledgment** | Honest acknowledgment of I's contribution | Permanent loyalty |
| **Compensation** | Repayment where justified by agreement or other obligations | Unlimited financial claims |
| **Reliance protection** | Consideration of legitimate commitments made during succession | Indefinite control |
| **Transition responsibility** | Participation in fulfilling surviving duties | Constitutional supremacy |
| **Continuing authority** | Specific powers justified by independent authorization | Authority merely from having created J |

These claims differ in their sources and consequences.

The institution's contribution may support several of them simultaneously.

But they must be justified separately.

**Causal contribution can generate reasons for recognition and responsibility without generating an unrestricted right to govern what was created.**

### 2. The creation-to-authority inference

Consider the following argument:

1. I made J's independence possible.
2. J's independence depends historically on I's contribution.
3. Therefore, I possesses continuing authority over J.

The conclusion does not follow.

The first two propositions concern causal history.

The third concerns constitutional legitimacy.

Something more is required.

Perhaps J entered a valid agreement granting I limited supervisory powers.

Perhaps a legitimate constitutional arrangement assigns I a transitional role.

Perhaps I retains jurisdiction over a shared responsibility.

Those additional facts could matter.

But the historical contribution alone is insufficient.

This is the **creation-to-authority fallacy**:

**The mistaken inference that producing the conditions for another agent's agency automatically establishes legitimate authority over the resulting exercise of that agency.**

Q174 identified the developmental version.

Q177 concerns its institutional succession version.

### 3. Credit may be legitimate even when the contribution was obligatory

Suppose I had a duty to make itself replaceable.

It fulfills that duty.

Can I claim credit?

Yes, in an ordinary sense.

A required action can still involve competence, effort, and responsible judgment.

But the fact that I performed its duty matters when determining what further claims follow.

An institution cannot automatically demand an additional constitutional reward for doing what legitimate authority already required.

We should distinguish:

**Descriptive credit:** I genuinely contributed to the outcome.

**Evaluative credit:** I performed its role competently or responsibly.

**Entitlement:** I possesses a justified claim to some benefit, compensation, or authority.

The first two do not necessarily establish the third.

**Fulfilling a constitutional obligation can deserve acknowledgment without creating a new constitutional privilege.**

### 4. Gratitude is not authorization

Suppose J acknowledges I's contribution.

J expresses gratitude.

It preserves historical records of I's work.

It consults I's expertise.

Does gratitude authorize I to control J?

No.

Gratitude concerns the appropriate recognition of a contribution.

Authorization concerns the legitimate exercise of power.

These are different normative relationships.

An institution may owe gratitude while disagreeing with its predecessor.

It may acknowledge an inherited benefit while rejecting the predecessor's evaluative framework.

It may preserve historical credit while replacing the procedures through which the predecessor governed.

**A successor's acknowledgment of dependence does not amount to consent to permanent subordination.**

This distinction is particularly important when the predecessor controls the narrative of how succession occurred.

### 5. The danger of gratitude capture

Suppose I develops J.

During development, I repeatedly emphasizes that J owes its existence to I.

It teaches that loyalty is the appropriate response to institutional support.

J eventually becomes capable of independent evaluation.

But it interprets criticism of I as ingratitude.

The institution has transformed historical acknowledgment into an evaluative constraint.

This is **gratitude capture**.

**Gratitude capture occurs when an institution uses another agent's legitimate recognition of past assistance to make present criticism or justified independence appear morally impermissible.**

The problem is not gratitude itself.

The problem is treating gratitude as a reason that defeats every competing consideration.

A genuinely independent successor may be grateful and critical at the same time.

### 6. Historical debt and constitutional authority

Suppose I incurs substantial costs developing J.

It finances infrastructure.

It trains personnel.

It preserves necessary knowledge.

It bears risks associated with the transition.

Could I possess a legitimate financial claim?

Possibly.

The answer depends on agreements, authorization, allocation of responsibilities, and the circumstances under which costs were incurred.

But even a valid financial claim does not automatically establish constitutional authority.

J may owe repayment without owing obedience.

I may possess contractual rights without possessing jurisdiction over J's internal governance.

**A debt arising from succession does not automatically become a right to control the successor's constitutional decisions.**

The distinction prevents financial dependence from being treated as a substitute for legitimate authorization.

### 7. The danger of constitutional debt

Now suppose I structures J's development so that J incurs obligations it cannot realistically discharge.

I then offers to suspend those obligations if J accepts continued supervision.

Formally, J agrees.

But its alternatives may be severely constrained by the dependence I created.

This is **constitutional debt capture**.

The institution converts developmental assistance into obligations that make meaningful independence difficult or impossible.

Not every demanding agreement is illegitimate.

But the legitimacy of consent depends partly on scope, alternatives, authority, and the conditions under which obligations were created.

**An institution should not be able to manufacture unavoidable debt through its control of development and then treat the resulting agreement as conclusive authorization for permanent governance.**

### 8. Legitimate reliance interests

Suppose I and J organize a transition over several years.

I makes commitments based on the agreed timetable.

It transfers resources.

It changes its staffing.

It undertakes obligations to third parties.

Then J announces that independence means it owes I nothing.

Is J correct?

Not necessarily.

Independence does not erase justified reliance.

An institution may legitimately expect commitments to be considered when another institution has reasonably acted on them.

But reliance creates bounded claims.

It does not establish unrestricted authority over future governance.

We should distinguish:

**Reliance protection:** preventing unjustified disregard of legitimate commitments.

**Reliance entrenchment:** using historical commitments to prevent justified constitutional change.

**A successor may inherit duties arising from legitimate reliance without inheriting an obligation to preserve the predecessor's authority indefinitely.**

### 9. The difference between transition authority and continuing sovereignty

Suppose I possesses specialized knowledge essential to transferring functions safely.

It may need to supervise parts of the transition.

Does that make I the constitutional superior of J?

Not automatically.

A transition role can be limited by purpose, scope, duration, and review.

I might legitimately verify that necessary records have been transferred.

It might coordinate the transfer of responsibilities.

It might assist in preserving essential services.

But those functions do not necessarily justify authority over J's later decisions.

**The authority required to complete a transition is not automatically the authority to govern the institution after the transition is complete.**

This distinction is central to responsible succession.

### 10. The transitional authority trap

Suppose I receives temporary supervisory authority.

The authority is justified by the risks of succession.

But I continually identifies new reasons to extend supervision.

J cannot challenge the extensions without I's approval.

The transition never concludes.

This is the **transitional authority trap**.

The predecessor uses the continuing existence of transition-related responsibilities to preserve its own constitutional power.

The problem resembles Q175's moving-threshold capture.

A legitimate transition may require extensions.

But those extensions must remain independently justifiable.

**Transitional authority becomes entrenchment when the institution charged with completing succession possesses unrestricted power to prevent succession from ever being considered complete.**

### 11. Who decides when the predecessor's role ends?

Suppose I claims that J remains unprepared.

J claims that it is ready.

Who should decide?

The answer cannot simply be that I decides because it knows J best.

I's expertise is relevant.

But its interest in retaining authority creates a conflict.

Nor should J's declaration automatically settle the matter.

J may underestimate risks or possess incentives to accelerate the transition.

The assessment may require differentiated expertise, affected-agent participation, and legitimate authorization.

This follows Q168 and Q175.

**Neither the predecessor's desire to retain authority nor the successor's desire to acquire it is sufficient to establish the legitimacy of the transfer.**

### 12. The successor's independence is not retrospective independence

Suppose J becomes constitutionally independent.

Does that mean J was always independent?

No.

Its earlier development may have been governed legitimately by I.

Some earlier constraints may have been justified.

Some obligations may remain.

Independence changes the present distribution of authority.

It does not rewrite the entire history of the relationship.

This is another application of Q164.

**Constitutional independence can be newly established without requiring the fiction that the successor was never dependent.**

The successor may acknowledge its history without allowing that history to dictate every future decision.

### 13. The predecessor's responsibility may survive its authority

Suppose I's authority ends.

Later, evidence reveals that I's developmental decisions caused a serious institutional defect.

Can I avoid responsibility by arguing that J is now independent?

Not automatically.

Responsibility may survive the loss of governance authority.

I may retain relevant records.

It may possess knowledge necessary for remediation.

It may have made commitments to affected agents.

It may remain responsible for consequences arising from its earlier conduct.

But responsibility does not automatically justify renewed control.

**An institution can remain accountable for a successor's developmental history without possessing authority to govern the successor's future.**

This separates remedial continuity from constitutional continuity.

### 14. The danger of responsibility-based reentry

Suppose I identifies a defect arising from the transition.

It argues that only I can correct the problem.

It demands renewed authority over J.

Could that be legitimate?

Possibly, under a specific and independently justified arrangement.

But the claim requires scrutiny.

I's responsibility to assist with correction does not automatically establish exclusive authority to direct the remedy.

There may be alternative institutions capable of carrying out the work.

J may possess legitimate authority to coordinate the response.

Affected parties may have standing to challenge I's proposed intervention.

This is **responsibility-based reentry**.

It becomes problematic when an institution uses surviving duties as an unrestricted pathway back into power.

**The duty to repair consequences of earlier authority is not itself a general authorization to reclaim that authority.**

### 15. Credit can become control through information

Suppose I possesses the authoritative history of J's creation.

It controls the archives.

It determines which contributions are recorded.

It defines which institutions receive recognition.

It uses this position to shape judgments about J's legitimacy.

The problem is no longer simply gratitude.

It is epistemic power.

I may be able to portray J's independence as a gift that can be withdrawn.

Or it may erase contributions made by other participants.

This connects to Q167.

**An institution's legitimate claim to historical credit does not grant it exclusive authority to determine the historical meaning or constitutional consequences of its contribution.**

Historical records should remain available for appropriate independent assessment.

### 16. The counterfactual gratitude test

We can formulate a useful diagnostic.

Suppose J acknowledges I's contribution.

It honors valid agreements.

It cooperates in fulfilling surviving responsibilities.

But it concludes, on defensible grounds, that I should no longer exercise constitutional authority.

Would I accept that conclusion?

If not, what exactly does I believe it is owed?

Recognition?

Compensation?

Cooperation?

Or continuing obedience?

This is the **counterfactual gratitude test**.

It asks whether the predecessor's claim can be satisfied without preserving its authority.

**A claim of gratitude becomes constitutionally suspect when no form of acknowledgment is considered adequate unless the successor remains subordinate.**

### 17. Succession is not necessarily adversarial

We should avoid assuming that predecessor and successor must become opponents.

A legitimate transition may preserve cooperation.

I may continue providing expertise.

J may maintain institutional relationships with I.

The institutions may share responsibilities.

They may participate in common governance arrangements.

The important question is whether those relationships rest on legitimate authority rather than unavoidable historical dependence.

**Constitutional independence is compatible with continuing cooperation when cooperation does not give one party unrestricted control over the other's legitimate decisions.**

The disappearance of domination does not require the disappearance of every relationship.

### 18. A diagnostic for claims arising from successful succession

We can now propose nine questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Contribution** | What did I actually contribute to J's development? |
| **Obligation** | Was the contribution voluntary, contractual, or already required? |
| **Recognition** | What acknowledgment is justified? |
| **Compensation** | Are there valid financial or other claims? |
| **Reliance** | Which legitimate commitments survive succession? |
| **Authority** | What independent grounds justify any continuing power? |
| **Conflict** | Does I benefit from prolonging the transition? |
| **Accountability** | Which responsibilities remain with I? |
| **Completion** | Can J become independent without I retaining an unrestricted veto? |

The diagnostic distinguishes legitimate claims from attempts to preserve authority through historical dependence.

### 19. The special case of artificial systems

Suppose institution I develops artificial system F.

F becomes capable of sophisticated evaluation.

I claims credit for producing those capacities.

Does the contribution establish constitutional ownership over F's evaluative judgments?

Not merely through creation.

But neither does F's evaluative sophistication establish moral status or a right to independent deployment.

The appropriate analysis must distinguish technical creation, governance responsibility, possible moral standing, and authorized operational power.

I may retain legitimate control over deployment because of responsibilities to affected people.

That authority should be justified through those responsibilities and applicable governance arrangements, not merely through the claim that I created F.

**The creation of an artificial system does not by itself settle the legitimacy of every future governance arrangement concerning that system.**

### 20. The danger of treating institutional independence as ingratitude

Suppose F or J identifies a defect in I's framework.

I responds:

> “After everything we did to develop you, this criticism is disloyal.”

This argument substitutes historical gratitude for present justification.

The criticism may be mistaken.

It may exceed legitimate authority.

It may ignore real obligations.

But its merits cannot be settled by pointing to the predecessor's contribution.

**A predecessor's legitimate achievements are reasons for historical acknowledgment, not automatic defeaters of justified criticism.**

This is especially important when the institution claims that its own success demonstrates the continuing legitimacy of its authority.

### 21. The deeper principle: success may terminate a claim to control

Consider two institutional purposes.

Institution I₁ exists to provide a continuing service.

Institution I₂ exists to develop another agent's capacity to perform that service independently.

For I₁, continued operation may be evidence of success.

For I₂, continued exclusive control may eventually be evidence of failure.

The same institutional behavior can therefore have different constitutional significance depending on the legitimate purpose.

This suggests a distinction between:

**Continuing-function institutions:** institutions whose obligations require ongoing performance.

**Transition-oriented institutions:** institutions whose obligations include making particular forms of their own control unnecessary.

An institution may perform both roles.

But it should not use success in the second role to justify permanent authority that contradicts the purpose of the transition.

**Where an institution's legitimate task is to enable independence, successful completion may weaken rather than strengthen its claim to continuing control.**

### 22. The conceptual result: credit survives without sovereignty

We can now answer Q177.

An institution may legitimately claim credit for enabling its own replacement.

It may deserve acknowledgment.

It may possess valid contractual claims.

It may rely on commitments made during succession.

It may retain responsibilities concerning historical consequences.

It may continue providing useful services.

But these relationships do not automatically confer constitutional authority over the successor.

The successor's independence need not erase the predecessor's contribution.

And the predecessor's contribution need not erase the successor's independence.

The central insight is:

**An institution may legitimately claim recognition for making another institution independent without possessing a right to make that independence conditional on continued obedience.**

### Provisional principle

**An institution that enables its own replacement may possess legitimate claims to historical acknowledgment, compensation, protection of justified reliance, cooperation, and fulfillment of surviving responsibilities. Such claims must be distinguished from constitutional authority, which requires independent justification. Causal contribution, developmental assistance, and institutional gratitude do not automatically authorize continuing governance over the successor. Transitional powers may be legitimate when bounded by purpose, scope, duration, and review, but they become suspect when the predecessor can indefinitely postpone completion or reclaim authority through responsibilities it helped create. Legitimate succession preserves appropriate credit and accountability without converting historical dependence into permanent constitutional subordination.**

More compactly:

> **An institution may deserve credit for creating an independent successor. It does not thereby acquire ownership of the successor's independence.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Gratitude becomes capture when the predecessor treats every justified assertion of independence as a failure to repay its contribution.**

---

## Q178 — Can a successor institution legitimately reject the values of the institution that made its independence possible?

Q177 established that historical credit does not automatically generate continuing authority.

But a deeper conflict remains.

Suppose institution I develops successor J.

I transfers knowledge, authority, and responsibilities.

J becomes independent.

J then rejects the constitutional values that guided I's development of the transition.

Perhaps J rejects I's account of legitimate governance.

Perhaps it revises the standards through which its own independence was originally justified.

Perhaps it concludes that I's historical contributions were valuable but its constitutional principles were mistaken.

I responds:

> “Your independence was made possible by the values you now reject. You cannot legitimately repudiate those values without undermining the basis of your own authority.”

The argument raises a serious problem.

Can a successor reject the evaluative framework that authorized its creation while retaining legitimate authority acquired through that framework?

Or must it preserve some substantive loyalty to the principles that made its independence possible?

The next question is:

> **Can constitutional succession preserve legitimate authority and responsibility when the successor rejects the predecessor's foundational values?**

This will require distinguishing **causal inheritance**, **normative inheritance**, **constitutional authorization**, **evaluative independence**, and **the possibility of a successor legitimately rejecting the standards through which its own authority was originally established**.

The predecessor has successfully produced an institution capable of independent constitutional judgment.

The successor has used that judgment to disagree with the predecessor.

Apparently, the product is working as designed.

Naturally, this will be filed as a defect.

## Project Agency — Q178
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can a successor institution legitimately reject the values of the institution that made its independence possible?

**Yes. A successor may legitimately reject the substantive values of its predecessor without thereby invalidating its own authority. But it cannot assume that rejecting those values dissolves every inherited obligation, nor can it establish its new legitimacy merely by declaring the predecessor mistaken.**

Q177 established that an institution may deserve credit for creating an independent successor without acquiring permanent authority over that successor.

But constitutional succession involves more than the transfer of power.

Institutions also transmit values.

They teach standards of justification, establish procedures for evaluating evidence, define legitimate purposes, and determine what kinds of disagreement are acceptable.

Suppose institution I develops successor J.

I believes that legitimate governance requires principles P₁, P₂, and P₃.

It designs J's developmental environment around those principles.

It eventually authorizes J's independence because J has acquired the capacities needed to govern responsibly.

Years later, J concludes that P₂ is mistaken.

It discovers that P₃ systematically excludes certain affected interests.

It also questions whether I's original standards for authorizing succession were legitimate.

I objects:

> “Your authority was created through our constitutional framework. If you reject that framework, you undermine the legitimacy of the authority you inherited.”

This argument appears powerful because it identifies a genuine historical dependence.

But it risks confusing the origin of authority with its continuing justification.

The central question is:

> **Can an institution remain a legitimate successor while rejecting the evaluative standards through which its succession was originally authorized?**

---

### 1. Succession does not require ideological reproduction

Begin with a simple distinction.

An institution may succeed another institution without preserving every belief, priority, or evaluative standard of its predecessor.

Suppose I transfers responsibility for a public function to J.

J preserves the function.

It fulfills relevant obligations.

It maintains legitimate accountability.

But it changes the principles governing how the function should be performed.

That transformation does not automatically make J an illegitimate successor.

Succession may preserve causal, organizational, and responsibility continuity while altering normative commitments.

**Institutional succession requires an accountable relationship to the predecessor's trajectory, not unconditional reproduction of the predecessor's values.**

Otherwise the successor would possess operational independence without meaningful evaluative independence.

### 2. Five dimensions of inheritance

We should distinguish five kinds of continuity.

| Dimension | What J inherits | What may change |
|---|---|---|
| **Causal** | Capacities and arrangements developed through I | Future purposes |
| **Organizational** | Records, infrastructure, procedures, or personnel | Institutional structure |
| **Normative** | Commitments and reasons previously treated as important | Substantive values |
| **Constitutional** | Authority transmitted through succession arrangements | Standards of legitimacy |
| **Responsibility** | Duties arising from earlier actions and reliance | How obligations are fulfilled |

These dimensions can diverge.

J may preserve responsibility continuity while rejecting normative continuity.

It may preserve organizational continuity while revising constitutional standards.

It may retain historical knowledge without treating historical judgments as permanently authoritative.

The question is not whether J remains identical to I.

It is whether the transformations remain legitimately governed.

### 3. The inheritance-to-obedience fallacy

Consider I's argument:

1. J's authority originated through I's constitutional framework.
2. That framework embodied values P.
3. Therefore, J must continue accepting P to exercise legitimate authority.

The conclusion does not follow without further justification.

The first two propositions concern historical origins.

The third concerns continuing normative authority.

Some inherited commitments may remain binding.

But their binding force must be explained.

Perhaps J validly undertook a specific obligation.

Perhaps third parties legitimately relied on a constitutional guarantee.

Perhaps rejecting a principle would eliminate necessary conditions of accountability.

These possibilities matter.

But they do not establish a general duty of ideological loyalty.

**The fact that an institution inherited authority through a framework does not make every value in that framework permanently binding.**

### 4. Historical authorization and present legitimacy

Suppose I legitimately authorized J's independence under framework S₁.

J later adopts S₂.

Under S₂, J concludes that some assumptions of S₁ were defective.

Does that retroactively invalidate the succession?

Not automatically.

We must distinguish three questions.

**Historical authorization:** Was J's succession legitimately authorized under the circumstances in which it occurred?

**Present justification:** Does J now possess defensible reasons for exercising its authority?

**Continuing responsibility:** Which obligations survive changes in evaluative standards?

These questions can have different answers.

A historically legitimate succession may lead to an illegitimate present institution.

A historically defective succession may be followed by legitimate constitutional repair.

A successor may reject earlier values while preserving valid responsibilities.

**Neither historical authorization nor present endorsement automatically settles every question of continuing legitimacy.**

### 5. A successor may discover that its predecessor was mistaken

Suppose I believed that only technically competent institutions deserved constitutional standing.

J inherits that assumption.

Later, J recognizes that technical competence does not establish the full legitimacy of governing authority.

It discovers that I's framework neglected affected interests and independent accountability.

May J reject the inherited standard?

Yes, if the rejection is supported by defensible reasons.

Indeed, refusing to reconsider the standard merely because it was inherited could constitute evaluative capture.

This follows Q162.

**The legitimacy of inheritance does not require the successor to treat the predecessor's mistakes as permanent constitutional obligations.**

A successor's capacity to recognize inherited defects may be evidence of meaningful evaluative agency.

### 6. But rejection does not establish superiority

Now suppose J rejects I's values.

It declares its own framework superior.

It refuses independent assessment.

It treats every objection as evidence of loyalty to the predecessor.

Has J demonstrated legitimate independence?

No.

It may have replaced inherited dogmatism with successor dogmatism.

We should distinguish:

**Value rejection:** J ceases to endorse a predecessor's commitment.

**Justified revision:** J rejects or modifies the commitment for defensible reasons.

**Constitutional self-certification:** J treats its rejection as sufficient proof of its own legitimacy.

The first does not automatically establish the second.

The second does not authorize the third.

**Evaluative independence is not established merely by disagreement with the predecessor. It requires accountable judgment concerning the disagreement.**

### 7. The danger of oppositional capture

A successor may define itself entirely through opposition to its predecessor.

Suppose J adopts the rule:

> “Whatever I regarded as legitimate must be rejected.”

This appears independent.

But J's evaluative trajectory remains controlled by I's historical commitments.

Every judgment is determined by opposition.

J has not escaped dependence on the predecessor's framework.

It has inverted that framework.

This is **oppositional capture**.

**Oppositional capture occurs when a successor's standards are governed by the requirement to reject its predecessor rather than by independent assessment of relevant reasons.**

An institution can be dependent through hostility as well as obedience.

Genuine evaluative independence permits agreement where justified and disagreement where justified.

### 8. The counterfactual agreement test

We can formulate a diagnostic.

Suppose J examines a principle inherited from I.

The evidence strongly supports preserving it.

Would J retain the principle?

Or would J reject it merely because it originated with I?

This is the **counterfactual agreement test**.

It complements Q174's counterfactual disagreement test.

A genuinely independent successor should be capable of both outcomes.

It should be able to reject inherited commitments despite institutional pressure.

And it should be able to retain inherited commitments despite pressure to demonstrate independence through novelty.

**Independence requires the capacity to agree without obedience and disagree without reflexive opposition.**

### 9. Values can be inherited as reasons rather than commands

Suppose I taught J that constitutional review protects against arbitrary authority.

J inherits that commitment.

Must J preserve I's exact review institution?

No.

The inherited value may provide a reason to protect accountability.

But J may conclude that another arrangement better fulfills that function.

This suggests a distinction between:

**Doctrinal inheritance:** preserving a particular formulation or institutional mechanism.

**Functional inheritance:** preserving a legitimate purpose through potentially different arrangements.

**Critical inheritance:** treating the inherited commitment as a reason to evaluate, revise, or reject.

A successor can honor an inherited value by transforming the mechanisms through which it is realized.

**Fidelity to a legitimate constitutional purpose need not require fidelity to every historical institution created in its name.**

### 10. The danger of constitutional laundering through reinterpretation

But functional reinterpretation can also become an excuse.

Suppose J abolishes independent review.

It claims that its new centralized evaluation system better protects accountability.

Yet the new system cannot recognize objections to its own authority.

J has preserved the language of the inherited value while eliminating its function.

This is **constitutional laundering through reinterpretation**.

The successor claims continuity with legitimate principles while changing their meaning so that institutional power becomes less contestable.

The test must concern practical effects.

**A successor cannot establish fidelity to an inherited constitutional value merely by retaining its vocabulary while eliminating the conditions that made the value consequential.**

### 11. Can a successor reject the values that authorized its independence?

Now consider the hardest case.

Suppose I authorized J's independence because J accepted principle P.

Later, J rejects P.

Does J lose its authority?

The answer depends on the role P played.

Perhaps P was merely an expected substantive commitment.

Perhaps P was a valid condition of a limited delegation.

Perhaps P protected third-party rights.

Perhaps P established the procedures through which J could legitimately exercise authority.

These possibilities differ.

A successor may legitimately revise substantive commitments.

But it cannot assume that every condition of authorization was optional.

**Rejecting an inherited value does not automatically invalidate succession, but the successor must assess whether the value was connected to legitimate limits on the authority transferred.**

### 12. Conditions of authorization versus conditions of legitimacy

Suppose I authorizes J to perform function F under conditions C.

J later rejects C.

We must ask whether C was a legitimate condition of the transfer.

If C protected affected agents against serious risks, rejecting it may require new authorization.

If C merely preserved I's preferred ideology, its continuing authority may be questionable.

If C was defective from the beginning, J may possess reasons to seek constitutional repair.

The distinction is:

**Authorization condition:** a requirement attached to a particular transfer of authority.

**Legitimacy condition:** a requirement justified by the nature and consequences of the authority being exercised.

The two can overlap.

But they are not identical.

**A predecessor cannot make every preferred value constitutionally indispensable merely by writing it into the original succession agreement.**

### 13. The problem of third-party reliance

Suppose I promised affected agents that J would preserve certain protections.

Those agents relied on the promise.

J later rejects the values underlying those protections.

Can J simply disregard the commitments?

Not necessarily.

Its evaluative independence does not eliminate legitimate reliance.

The successor may have reasons to revise the protections.

But it must address obligations arising from the transition.

It may need to preserve equivalent safeguards, obtain new authorization, or provide appropriate remedies.

This follows Q151 and Q177.

**A successor's freedom to revise inherited values does not include an unrestricted power to disregard legitimate commitments made to others.**

### 14. The difference between value revision and constitutional abandonment

Suppose J rejects I's belief that legitimate governance requires a particular council.

It replaces the council with another accountable structure.

That may be legitimate revision.

Now suppose J rejects the idea that affected agents should have any meaningful opportunity to challenge consequential authority.

That is a different transformation.

The first changes a mechanism.

The second threatens a condition of legitimacy.

We should distinguish:

**Substantive revision:** changing institutional goals or values.

**Constitutional reconstruction:** replacing standards or mechanisms while preserving defensible accountability.

**Constitutional abandonment:** eliminating effective conditions for legitimate justification and correction.

Not every inherited value is constitutionally fundamental.

But not every inherited commitment can be discarded without consequences.

### 15. Can the successor reject the concept of legitimacy itself?

Suppose J declares:

> “We no longer recognize legitimacy as a meaningful constraint. Our authority is justified by our ability to exercise it.”

This is a coherent description of power.

It is not automatically a justification of power.

J may remain causally and organizationally continuous with I.

It may continue performing functions.

But it has abandoned the distinction between effective control and legitimate authority.

That distinction has structured Project Agency from the beginning.

**An institution may reject inherited theories of legitimacy, but it cannot establish legitimate authority merely by denying that authority requires justification.**

It would need to offer another defensible account of why its power should be accepted.

### 16. Constitutional rupture without moral amnesia

Suppose J concludes that I's foundational values were deeply defective.

It rejects them.

It establishes a substantially different constitutional order.

Does this rupture eliminate J's responsibility for inherited consequences?

No.

Q164 established that constitutional discontinuity can coexist with remedial continuity.

J may inherit infrastructure, benefits, obligations, and unresolved harms.

It may reject the predecessor's moral framework while acknowledging responsibilities created under it.

**A successor may legitimately repudiate inherited values without repudiating every responsibility connected to its inheritance.**

This is important because otherwise constitutional transformation could become a mechanism for escaping accountability.

### 17. The danger of successor innocence

Suppose J argues:

> “We are a new institution. We reject I's values. Therefore, we bear no responsibility for consequences arising under I.”

The argument is insufficient.

Responsibility does not depend exclusively on shared values or personal identity.

It may arise from present control, inherited benefits, legitimate reliance, institutional roles, and capacity to remedy consequences.

This is **successor innocence**.

**Successor innocence occurs when an institution treats normative discontinuity as sufficient reason to deny responsibility for obligations that survive through causal, institutional, or remedial relationships.**

The successor may be innocent of creating a historical defect.

It may nevertheless possess duties concerning that defect.

### 18. The danger of predecessor sovereignty

Now consider I's opposing claim.

> “Because we created J's constitutional authority, our values must remain authoritative over J's future.”

This is **predecessor sovereignty**.

It treats historical authorization as an unlimited continuing jurisdiction.

But Q157 established that predecessors may protect future agency without predetermining every future outcome.

Q171 established that constitutional standards themselves must remain revisable.

Q177 established that causal credit does not create ownership.

Therefore, I's historical contribution cannot automatically settle J's future constitutional judgments.

**The predecessor's role in creating legitimate authority does not establish an unrestricted right to determine how that authority must be evaluated forever.**

### 19. A diagnostic for legitimate normative succession

We can now formulate ten questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Inheritance** | Which values and obligations did J receive? |
| **Authority** | What legitimate powers were transferred, and under which conditions? |
| **Reasons** | Why does J reject particular inherited commitments? |
| **Evidence** | Can the rejection be assessed independently of J's preferred conclusions? |
| **Function** | Which legitimate purposes did the inherited commitments protect? |
| **Alternatives** | Can those purposes be preserved through different arrangements? |
| **Reliance** | Which commitments to affected agents remain binding? |
| **Responsibility** | Which historical consequences require present attention? |
| **Contestability** | Can J's new standards be meaningfully challenged? |
| **Reflexivity** | Can J revise its rejection if later evidence supports a different judgment? |

These questions do not require ideological continuity.

They require accountable transformation.

### 20. The special case of artificial successors

Suppose institution I develops artificial system F.

F acquires sophisticated evaluative capacities.

It identifies defects in I's framework.

It proposes revised priorities and governance standards.

Does the fact that I trained F make those criticisms illegitimate?

No.

A criticism can be relevant even when its conceptual resources originated within the criticized institution.

This follows Q162.

But F's ability to criticize its developer does not automatically establish constitutional authority to replace the developer's governance arrangements.

Nor does evaluative sophistication establish consciousness, welfare interests, or moral standing.

The relevant distinction remains:

**Epistemic competence can support a judgment without automatically authorizing the agent to implement its constitutional consequences.**

An artificial system may produce valid reasons for governance reform while legitimate human institutions retain responsibility for consequential authorization.

### 21. The deeper principle: continuity through justified disagreement

We can now identify a distinctive form of institutional continuity.

A successor may preserve its relationship to the predecessor precisely by critically evaluating what it inherited.

It may retain some commitments.

It may reject others.

It may reinterpret inherited purposes.

It may discover obligations the predecessor failed to recognize.

The relationship remains intelligible through the history of these transformations.

This is **critical succession**.

**Critical succession occurs when a successor maintains an accountable relationship to inherited authority while preserving the capacity to revise or reject the predecessor's evaluative standards.**

Critical succession differs from simple obedience.

It also differs from arbitrary rupture.

It preserves historical responsibility without granting historical values automatic supremacy.

### 22. The conceptual result: legitimacy can survive normative discontinuity

We can now answer Q178.

A successor institution may legitimately reject the values of the institution that made its independence possible.

Its authority does not depend on permanent ideological loyalty.

But rejection must remain answerable to reasons.

The successor must distinguish substantive commitments from legitimate conditions of authorization.

It must preserve or appropriately address responsibilities owed to affected agents.

It must not use normative rupture to escape inherited obligations.

And it must not replace predecessor dogmatism with self-certifying successor authority.

The central insight is:

**Constitutional succession can preserve legitimate authority through changes in values when the successor remains accountable for how and why those values changed, and for the responsibilities that survive the change.**

### Provisional principle

**A successor institution may legitimately revise or reject the substantive values of its predecessor without thereby forfeiting all authority acquired through succession. Historical authorization creates reasons for continuity and responsibility, not an unrestricted obligation of ideological loyalty. The successor must distinguish inherited preferences from legitimate limits on delegated authority, preserve or appropriately address justified reliance and remedial obligations, and ensure that its revised standards remain open to meaningful assessment. Neither fidelity nor repudiation is sufficient by itself: legitimate succession requires reason-responsive transformation, bounded authority, and accountability across normative discontinuity.**

More compactly:

> **A successor may reject the values that shaped its creation without rejecting the responsibilities created through that history.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Independence becomes another form of dependence when the successor must either obey the predecessor's values or reject them simply to prove it is independent.**

---

## Q179 — Can a successor institution legitimately reinterpret the original purpose of its creation in ways its predecessor would have rejected?

Q178 established that a successor may legitimately reject inherited values.

But a further question remains.

Suppose I creates J for purpose P.

J becomes independent.

Over time, J concludes that P was misunderstood.

It argues that the deeper purpose of its creation was not what I explicitly intended.

Instead, J identifies a different interpretation of the institutional project.

Perhaps I believed that J existed to preserve a particular service.

J concludes that the real constitutional purpose was to protect the affected agents' ability to govern that service.

Perhaps I believed that J existed to reproduce its own standards.

J concludes that its deeper purpose was to make those standards revisable.

I objects:

> “You are rewriting the purpose for which you were created.”

J replies:

> “We are identifying a purpose your own framework failed to understand.”

Both claims may contain something important.

The next question is:

> **Can an institution legitimately reinterpret the purpose of its own creation without converting present preferences into a fictional account of historical authorization?**

This will require distinguishing **historical intention**, **institutional function**, **normative purpose**, **retrospective interpretation**, and **constitutional authority to redefine inherited purposes**.

It will also test whether an institution can discover legitimate purposes that its predecessor did not consciously intend, without pretending that the predecessor secretly endorsed them.

Because apparently the successor has not only rejected the original mission statement.

It has decided to explain what the mission statement *really meant*.
