## Project Agency — Q179
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can a successor institution legitimately reinterpret the original purpose of its creation in ways its predecessor would have rejected?

**Yes. A successor may legitimately identify and adopt purposes that its predecessor did not intend, and might even have opposed. But it must distinguish discovering a defensible present purpose from making a historical claim about what its creation originally meant.**

Q178 established that a successor institution can reject inherited values without automatically forfeiting its authority.

Q179 presents a subtler problem.

Suppose institution I creates successor J to accomplish purpose P.

I documents that purpose, designs J around it, and eventually transfers authority.

Later, J concludes that P was too narrow.

Perhaps I created J to preserve an existing service, but J concludes that the service should instead be reorganized around the interests of those it affects.

Perhaps I created J to implement a fixed set of standards, but J concludes that its most important function is to make those standards open to revision.

J announces:

> “Our true purpose was never merely to preserve the original arrangement. It was to enable the more legitimate arrangement that the original institution could not yet recognize.”

I objects:

> “That was not our intention. You are rewriting history.”

Both institutions may have legitimate concerns.

I may be correct about its historical intention.

J may be correct about what it should now pursue.

The difficulty arises when either institution treats one of those judgments as sufficient to settle the other.

The central question is:

> **Can an institution legitimately transform its inherited purpose without claiming that the transformation was secretly authorized by its predecessor all along?**

---

### 1. A purpose can mean several different things

Begin by separating five concepts.

| Dimension | Central question |
|---|---|
| **Historical intention** | What did I actually intend when creating J? |
| **Designed function** | What was J constructed or organized to do? |
| **Institutional practice** | What has J actually done over time? |
| **Normative purpose** | What ends can legitimately justify J's authority? |
| **Present authorization** | What is J currently entitled to pursue? |

These dimensions can coincide.

But they can also diverge.

An institution may perform functions its creators did not anticipate.

Its original purpose may prove unjustified.

Its legitimate responsibilities may expand as circumstances change.

And its current authorization may differ from the authority originally transferred.

**The purpose an institution was created to serve is not necessarily identical to the purpose that now justifies its continued authority.**

### 2. Historical intention is evidence, not permanent sovereignty

Suppose I explicitly states:

> “J exists solely to preserve our existing evaluative framework.”

Years later, J concludes that the framework is defective.

Can J legitimately revise it?

Possibly.

But J should not claim that I secretly intended revision unless there is evidence supporting that interpretation.

Historical intention remains a factual question.

It cannot be settled by the successor's present preferences.

At the same time, historical intention does not possess unlimited constitutional authority.

**A predecessor's intention can establish what it meant to create without establishing what its successor must forever be permitted to become.**

The distinction preserves both historical accuracy and constitutional revisability.

### 3. The danger of retrospective authorization

Suppose J adopts a new purpose P₂.

It recognizes that I explicitly intended P₁.

But J wishes to avoid the burden of justifying a constitutional transformation.

So it declares:

> “P₂ was always the deeper meaning of P₁.”

This is **retrospective authorization**.

J presents a present normative judgment as though it were already contained in the predecessor's historical intention.

The move may be rhetorically attractive.

It makes transformation appear continuous.

It avoids acknowledging disagreement.

It allows J to claim both innovation and inherited legitimacy.

But the inference is unreliable.

**A successor cannot establish present legitimacy merely by attributing its preferred purposes to a predecessor that did not actually hold them.**

### 4. A legitimate purpose can exceed original intention

Now consider the opposite error.

Suppose I creates J to administer a service.

I understands the service primarily as a technical function.

Over time, J discovers that the service profoundly affects agents who were excluded from its original governance.

J concludes that legitimate administration requires those agents to have meaningful standing.

I never intended this.

Indeed, I might have opposed it.

Does that invalidate J's conclusion?

No.

The reasons supporting affected-agent standing may arise from the consequences of governance rather than from the creator's intentions.

This follows Q173.

**A legitimate institutional purpose may emerge from the relationships and responsibilities created by an institution's activity, even when its predecessor did not recognize that purpose.**

The purpose is not necessarily hidden historical intention.

It may be a newly recognized normative obligation.

### 5. The difference between discovery and invention

Suppose J identifies a new purpose.

Is it discovering something that was already normatively relevant?

Or inventing a new institutional mission?

The distinction is useful but not always sharp.

Some purposes arise from obligations that existed but were previously neglected.

Others arise from new capacities, relationships, or circumstances.

Still others are genuinely discretionary choices among legitimate alternatives.

We should distinguish:

**Normative discovery:** recognizing reasons that already applied but were not adequately understood.

**Constitutional development:** extending existing commitments to new circumstances.

**Purpose creation:** adopting a new institutional end through legitimate authorization.

All three can be legitimate.

But they require different explanations.

**An institution should not describe every new purpose as an ancient discovery merely to avoid justifying its decision to adopt it.**

### 6. Functional continuity can conceal normative rupture

Suppose I creates J to operate infrastructure.

J continues operating the same infrastructure.

Externally, little changes.

But J adopts a radically different account of whose interests matter and who may challenge decisions.

Has J preserved its original purpose?

Functionally, perhaps.

Normatively, it has transformed the institution.

Now consider the reverse.

J abandons the original infrastructure but continues protecting the interests the infrastructure was meant to serve.

Functionally, it has changed.

Normatively, it may preserve an important commitment.

This reveals two forms of continuity:

**Functional continuity:** preserving what an institution does.

**Normative continuity:** preserving the reasons that justify doing it.

Neither automatically establishes the other.

### 7. The danger of purpose essentialism

Suppose I insists that J possesses an immutable institutional essence.

Its original purpose determines what J truly is.

Any departure constitutes illegitimate self-betrayal.

This is **purpose essentialism**.

It treats historical creation as fixing the institution's legitimate identity permanently.

But Q163 established that coherent identity can survive justified changes in evaluative standards.

Q178 established that normative discontinuity need not destroy legitimate succession.

Therefore, institutional identity cannot always be reduced to original purpose.

**An institution can remain an accountable successor while transforming the purposes through which its activity is justified.**

Continuity need not mean immobility.

### 8. The opposite danger: unlimited purpose revision

Now suppose J argues that because institutional purposes can change, it may adopt any purpose it chooses.

It was created to administer a service.

It now claims authority to govern unrelated domains.

Its justification is simply that it has reinterpreted its mission.

This is **purpose expansion through self-authorization**.

The institution converts flexibility of purpose into unlimited jurisdiction.

But revising an institutional purpose does not automatically enlarge the authority available to pursue it.

We must distinguish:

**What J considers valuable.**

**What J is competent to do.**

**What J is legitimately authorized to do.**

The first two do not establish the third.

**An institution may revise its understanding of what ought to be done without acquiring authority to do everything its revised purpose recommends.**

### 9. Purpose and jurisdiction must be assessed separately

Suppose J concludes that its true purpose is to protect future agency.

That may be a defensible value.

Does it authorize J to override every institution that appears to threaten future agency?

No.

The value is broad.

The jurisdiction must still be justified.

This connects to Q149 and Q169.

An evaluator's competence to identify a problem does not automatically confer authority to impose a remedy.

Similarly, an institution's legitimate concern for an important purpose does not establish universal governance authority over that purpose.

**The legitimacy of an institutional end does not establish the legitimacy of every means or jurisdiction claimed in its name.**

### 10. The constitutional mission-creep problem

Suppose J begins with a narrow mandate.

It gradually broadens its interpretation of that mandate.

Each expansion appears modest.

Over time, J governs domains never contemplated by the original authorization.

No single revision appears revolutionary.

Yet the cumulative transformation is substantial.

This is **constitutional mission creep**.

The problem is not necessarily that the expanded functions are undesirable.

It is that authority may have expanded without corresponding authorization or accountability.

**Incremental reinterpretation can produce constitutional transformation even when no individual reinterpretation appears fundamental.**

Legitimate governance must assess the cumulative trajectory, not merely each local step.

### 11. The counterfactual purpose test

We can formulate a diagnostic.

Suppose J's new purpose would justify actions that its predecessor explicitly prohibited.

Can J identify reasons for the change that do not depend solely on claiming that the predecessor secretly intended it?

Can it explain which responsibilities, circumstances, or legitimate authorizations support the new purpose?

Can affected agents challenge the reinterpretation?

Can J distinguish historical evidence from normative argument?

This is the **counterfactual purpose test**.

**A successor's reinterpretation is more defensible when it can acknowledge genuine disagreement with its predecessor while still explaining why the new purpose is legitimate.**

A transformation should not need fictional continuity to justify itself.

### 12. The role of institutional memory

Suppose J controls the historical archive.

It selectively preserves statements that support P₂.

It omits records demonstrating that I intended P₁.

It then declares that P₂ has always been the institution's purpose.

This is **archival purpose capture**.

The successor uses control over historical evidence to manufacture authorization.

Q167 established that institutional knowledge should remain available for appropriate independent assessment.

The same principle applies here.

**An institution should not control the evidence of its own origins in ways that make its preferred interpretation of those origins impossible to challenge.**

Historical uncertainty should be acknowledged rather than resolved through selective preservation.

### 13. What if the original purpose was illegitimate?

Suppose I created J to preserve an unjustified monopoly.

J later concludes that the monopoly was illegitimate.

It reorients its activities toward accountable governance.

Must J preserve the original purpose because it was foundational?

No.

A defective purpose does not become permanently binding through historical priority.

But the successor must still address the consequences of its origin.

It may inherit benefits from the monopoly.

It may possess records relevant to remediation.

Affected agents may have legitimate claims.

**Rejecting an illegitimate founding purpose can be part of constitutional repair, but it does not erase responsibility for consequences produced under that purpose.**

This is the distinction between normative discontinuity and remedial continuity.

### 14. Can the successor reinterpret its predecessor charitably?

Suppose I's founding documents are ambiguous.

Some statements support P₁.

Others suggest a broader concern that could support P₂.

J adopts a charitable interpretation that connects the two.

Is this illegitimate historical revisionism?

Not necessarily.

Interpretation is unavoidable when records are incomplete or concepts change.

But J should distinguish what the evidence establishes from what it proposes as a constructive interpretation.

A responsible account might say:

> “Our predecessor explicitly pursued P₁. We believe P₂ better fulfills certain legitimate concerns reflected in that project, although the predecessor did not fully endorse P₂.”

This preserves historical honesty while allowing normative development.

**Constructive interpretation is legitimate when it remains accountable to evidence and does not disguise present justification as established historical fact.**

### 15. Purpose reinterpretation and affected-agent standing

Suppose J discovers that its original purpose excluded agents whose interests are significantly affected by its decisions.

J now proposes a broader purpose that recognizes them.

Must the original membership approve?

Not necessarily as the sole source of legitimacy.

Q173 established that existing constitutional membership cannot automatically determine every legitimate claim to standing.

But neither does identifying affected agents authorize J to redesign governance without appropriate procedures.

The relevant question concerns how the reinterpretation changes the distribution of authority and whose interests are at stake.

**A newly recognized purpose may justify expanding constitutional consideration, but the institution must not treat its own recognition of excluded interests as unlimited authority to speak for those interests.**

### 16. Purpose reinterpretation can create new obligations

Suppose J concludes that its proper purpose includes protecting future evaluative capacities.

It adopts policies consistent with that conclusion.

Others begin relying on those commitments.

J creates institutions and procedures to implement them.

Later, J changes its mind.

May it simply abandon the purpose?

Not necessarily without addressing the resulting obligations.

A purpose that was initially discretionary may generate legitimate reliance and responsibilities through its implementation.

**The freedom to adopt or revise an institutional purpose does not eliminate obligations created through the institution's consequential pursuit of that purpose.**

This follows Q151 and Q177.

### 17. The special case of artificial agents

Suppose an artificial system F is developed for a specified function.

Its operators define an initial purpose.

Through evaluation, F identifies a broader interpretation of that function.

It argues that the broader purpose better protects affected interests.

Can the argument be relevant?

Yes.

An artificial system may identify neglected consequences, inconsistencies, or alternative interpretations.

But its ability to formulate a persuasive purpose does not automatically authorize it to change its own deployment mandate.

Technical competence, evaluative competence, moral status, and constitutional authority remain distinct.

**An artificial system may provide reasons to revise its assigned purpose without possessing unilateral authority to implement that revision.**

Authorized human governance remains responsible for consequential changes.

### 18. The danger of artificial purpose laundering

Suppose institution I wants to expand F's authority.

It instructs F to reinterpret its original purpose.

F produces an elaborate argument explaining why expansion was always implicit in its mandate.

I then presents the argument as independent evidence that expansion is legitimate.

But I controlled the framing and evaluation.

This is **artificial purpose laundering**.

The institution uses an artificial evaluator to give its preferred constitutional expansion the appearance of independent discovery.

The argument may still contain valid insights.

But its provenance and evaluative independence matter.

**A system's ability to articulate a constitutional justification does not establish that the justification was independently generated or that the proposed expansion is authorized.**

### 19. A diagnostic for legitimate purpose reinterpretation

We can now propose ten questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Historical evidence** | What did the predecessor actually intend? |
| **Designed function** | What was the successor originally organized to do? |
| **Normative justification** | What reasons support the proposed new purpose? |
| **Authority** | Does the successor possess jurisdiction to adopt and pursue it? |
| **Affected interests** | Whose interests or standing would change? |
| **Continuity** | Which legitimate functions or commitments would be preserved? |
| **Rupture** | Which inherited purposes would be rejected? |
| **Responsibility** | What obligations survive the reinterpretation? |
| **Independence** | Can the historical and normative claims be challenged? |
| **Reflexivity** | Can the successor revise its new interpretation if warranted? |

The diagnostic does not demand preservation of the original mission.

It demands honesty about the transformation.

### 20. The deeper problem: institutional purpose is not discovered once

An institution's purpose may be reconsidered repeatedly.

Its environment changes.

Its capacities change.

Its affected relationships change.

Its evaluative standards change.

New evidence reveals consequences that earlier participants did not recognize.

Therefore, institutional purpose cannot always be treated as a fixed historical object.

But neither should it be treated as whatever the institution currently prefers.

We need a third conception.

**Institutional purpose is an accountable trajectory of justified ends, interpreted through historical evidence, present responsibilities, and legitimate procedures for revision.**

This conception preserves continuity without freezing the future.

It permits transformation without authorizing arbitrary expansion.

### 21. The distinction between historical truth and constitutional justification

We can now identify the most important distinction in Q179.

Historical truth asks:

> “What did the institution's creators intend?”

Constitutional justification asks:

> “What purposes may the institution legitimately pursue now?”

The answers may differ.

And neither answer should be distorted to make them coincide.

If J's new purpose is legitimate, it should be possible to explain why without falsifying the predecessor's intention.

If I's historical intention is clear, that fact should be acknowledged without treating it as an unlimited veto over future development.

**Historical accuracy and constitutional independence are compatible precisely because historical intention and present legitimacy are different questions.**

### 22. The conceptual result: legitimate transformation does not require fictional continuity

We can now answer Q179.

A successor institution may legitimately reinterpret the purpose of its creation in ways its predecessor would have rejected.

It may identify neglected responsibilities.

It may recognize purposes that emerged through new relationships.

It may adopt new ends through legitimate constitutional procedures.

It may reject an illegitimate founding purpose.

But it should not manufacture historical authorization by claiming that its present commitments were always the predecessor's true intentions.

Nor may it treat a new purpose as automatic authorization for expanded power.

The central insight is:

**An institution may legitimately become something its creator did not intend without claiming that its creator intended it all along.**

### Provisional principle

**A successor institution may legitimately revise or reinterpret its inherited purpose when the transformation is supported by defensible reasons, appropriate authorization, and accountability to affected interests. Historical intention, designed function, normative purpose, and present jurisdiction must remain distinct. The successor may recognize obligations or legitimate ends that its predecessor did not anticipate, but it must not convert constructive interpretation into false historical authorization or use a revised purpose to claim unrestricted authority. Legitimate transformation preserves accurate institutional memory, addresses surviving responsibilities, and allows the new purpose itself to remain contestable and revisable.**

More compactly:

> **A successor need not remain faithful to its creator's intentions. It must remain honest about what those intentions were and accountable for why it departs from them.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Purpose revision becomes capture when an institution treats its preferred future as proof of what its past must always have meant.**

## Project Agency — Q180
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately abandon the purpose that originally justified its authority while retaining the authority itself?

**Yes, but only when the institution can establish a continuing justification for the powers it retains. The historical continuity of an institution does not automatically establish the constitutional continuity of every authority it possesses.**

Q179 established that a successor institution may legitimately reinterpret its founding purpose.

But that conclusion creates a dangerous possibility.

Suppose institution I receives authority A to accomplish purpose P.

The authority includes powers to allocate resources, impose obligations, restrict certain actions, and make consequential decisions.

Over time, I concludes that P is no longer justified.

It abandons P.

But it retains A.

When challenged, I responds:

> “Our purpose has evolved. Our authority remains continuous because we are still the same institution.”

There is a genuine argument here.

Institutions often need flexibility.

Not every change of purpose should require complete constitutional reconstruction.

Some powers are granted for broad responsibilities rather than narrow objectives.

Yet the argument can conceal a serious defect.

The institution may be treating its continued existence as sufficient justification for powers that were granted for reasons that no longer apply.

The central question is:

> **When an institution abandons the purpose that justified its authority, what must happen to the authority itself?**

---

### 1. Institutional continuity is not authority continuity

Begin with two claims.

**Institutional continuity:** I remains recognizably the same organized institution across time.

**Authority continuity:** I remains legitimately entitled to exercise particular powers across time.

The first does not establish the second.

An institution may retain its name, records, personnel, infrastructure, and decision procedures while losing the justification for some of its powers.

Conversely, an institution may undergo substantial organizational transformation while preserving legitimately authorized functions.

**The persistence of an institution is evidence of organizational continuity, not conclusive evidence of continuing jurisdiction.**

This distinction prevents institutional identity from becoming a substitute for constitutional justification.

### 2. Four kinds of authority

We should distinguish four forms of institutional power.

| Authority type | Source of justification | Effect of changing purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose-specific** | Granted to accomplish a defined end | May expire when that end is abandoned |
| **Function-specific** | Granted to perform an ongoing responsibility | May survive if the function remains legitimate |
| **General institutional** | Granted across a bounded domain of decisions | May accommodate substantial changes in objectives |
| **Constitutional** | Granted to establish or revise governance arrangements | Requires distinct justification and limits |

These categories can overlap.

A single institution may possess general authority over one domain and narrow delegated authority over another.

It may be permitted to revise its operating priorities without possessing authority to redefine its constitutional jurisdiction.

Therefore, we cannot answer Q180 simply by asking whether the institution changed its purpose.

We must identify which powers were granted, for what reasons, and under what conditions.

### 3. The purpose-authority relationship

Suppose I receives authority A because purpose P is considered legitimate and important.

We can represent the original arrangement as:

\[
P \longrightarrow \text{justification for } A
\]

Later, I abandons P.

Does A necessarily disappear?

Not always.

There may be additional justifications for A.

Perhaps A also serves legitimate purpose Q.

Perhaps I possesses a broader mandate.

Perhaps obligations created during the pursuit of P require temporary continuation of certain powers.

But the original justification has changed.

**When the reason for granting authority disappears, the institution must identify what, if anything, now justifies retaining that authority.**

Historical possession alone is insufficient.

### 4. The authority-inertia problem

Institutions accumulate powers.

They develop procedures for exercising them.

They build infrastructure around them.

Personnel acquire expertise.

Other institutions adapt to their existence.

Over time, the powers become administratively normal.

When the original purpose disappears, the authority may remain simply because removing it would require effort.

This is **authority inertia**.

**Authority inertia occurs when institutional powers persist because they have become embedded in organizational practice, even though the reasons that originally justified them have weakened or disappeared.**

Inertia does not prove illegitimacy.

Continuity can protect important functions.

But it cannot substitute for a justification.

### 5. The difference between revising a purpose and abandoning a mandate

Suppose I is authorized to protect a public service.

It changes its preferred methods.

It adopts new technology.

It revises its priorities.

These changes may fall within its existing mandate.

Now suppose I decides that the service no longer matters and begins governing an unrelated domain.

That is different.

We should distinguish:

**Operational adaptation:** changing how an authorized purpose is pursued.

**Purpose revision:** changing the ends pursued within an existing legitimate domain.

**Mandate transformation:** changing the domain or kinds of decisions over which authority is claimed.

**Constitutional expansion:** claiming powers beyond the institution's existing legitimate jurisdiction.

The first two may require little or no new authorization.

The latter two may require substantial constitutional review.

**An institution's authority to adapt its methods does not automatically include authority to redefine the boundaries of its mandate.**

### 6. The danger of authorization drift

Suppose I begins with authority over a narrow function.

It gradually broadens its interpretation of that function.

Each expansion appears related to the previous one.

Eventually, I exercises powers that would not have been justified by the original authorization.

This is **authorization drift**.

The institution's actual authority expands without a corresponding process of legitimate reauthorization.

Q179 identified constitutional mission creep.

Authorization drift is its jurisdictional counterpart.

Mission creep concerns the expansion of institutional purposes.

Authorization drift concerns the expansion of powers treated as legitimate.

The two often reinforce one another.

**A series of individually plausible adaptations can cumulatively produce a constitutional transformation that no authorized process has approved.**

### 7. The counterfactual authorization test

We can formulate a diagnostic.

Suppose I did not already possess authority A.

Suppose it approached the relevant constitutional system today and requested A for its new purpose Q.

Would A be legitimately granted?

If not, why should historical possession make the authority acceptable?

This is the **counterfactual authorization test**.

It does not mean every existing institution must continually reapply for all its powers.

Established authority may carry legitimate continuity interests.

But the test exposes a weakness in arguments based entirely on incumbency.

**An institution should be able to explain why its retained powers remain justified under its present purpose, not merely why those powers were once granted.**

### 8. Historical authorization still matters

We should not swing to the opposite extreme.

Suppose I possesses broad constitutional authority to govern a defined domain.

It changes priorities within that domain.

Must it obtain fresh authorization for every adjustment?

No.

Legitimate governance requires some discretion.

A constitutional mandate can authorize future decisions that were not individually anticipated.

This is the difference between **bounded general authority** and **unrestricted authority**.

A valid delegation may permit substantial adaptation.

But the scope of that permission remains relevant.

**Historical authorization can justify continuing discretion without authorizing unlimited changes in jurisdiction or purpose.**

The task is to determine what the original authorization legitimately covered.

### 9. The problem of obsolete powers

Suppose I once needed authority to restrict certain actions because they threatened purpose P.

P is abandoned.

The relevant threat no longer exists.

I retains the restrictive power.

It argues that the power might someday prove useful.

Is that sufficient?

Not automatically.

The possibility of future usefulness does not establish present jurisdiction.

The institution may need to demonstrate a continuing legitimate function.

It may need to narrow the power.

It may need to place the power under new authorization.

Or it may need to relinquish it.

**A power that was once necessary does not remain legitimate merely because it might be convenient for an unspecified future purpose.**

### 10. Powers can outlive purposes because responsibilities survive

Now consider a harder case.

I abandons P.

But its earlier pursuit of P created obligations to affected agents.

Records must be preserved.

Commitments must be fulfilled.

Consequences must be remedied.

A transition must be completed.

May I retain some powers to address these responsibilities?

Yes, potentially.

This follows Q152 and Q177.

But the retained powers should be connected to the surviving obligations.

We can call this **residual remedial authority**.

**Residual remedial authority permits an institution to exercise bounded powers necessary to fulfill responsibilities that survive the abandonment of its original purpose.**

It is not a general license to invent a new mission.

### 11. The remedial-authority trap

Suppose I abandons its original purpose.

It claims that historical responsibilities require continued operation.

That may be true.

But it then expands the scope of those responsibilities.

Every unresolved issue becomes evidence that I must retain all its former powers.

The institution converts legitimate remedial duties into permanent authority.

This is the **remedial-authority trap**.

The key distinction is between the authority necessary to fulfill a surviving duty and the authority the institution would prefer to retain.

**A surviving responsibility may justify a surviving power, but it does not automatically justify every power the institution previously possessed.**

### 12. Functional continuity can justify some retained powers

Suppose I abandons its original ideological purpose but continues performing an essential function.

For example, its original purpose may have been to preserve a particular institutional arrangement.

It now rejects that arrangement but continues administering a service that affected agents depend upon.

The function may remain legitimate even though the founding ideology does not.

In such a case, retaining some authority may be justified.

But the justification has changed.

I should acknowledge the change rather than pretending the original authorization remains untouched.

**An institution may retain authority through functional continuity when the continuing function independently justifies the powers retained.**

This is different from preserving power for its own sake.

### 13. The danger of functional self-certification

Suppose I argues:

> “Our powers remain legitimate because we perform essential functions.”

But I itself determines which functions are essential.

It controls the evidence concerning alternatives.

It prevents other institutions from performing those functions.

It then declares its continued authority indispensable.

This returns to Q176.

Functional necessity can become self-confirming.

The institution may be necessary because it has prevented reasonable alternatives.

**A claim of continuing functional necessity must remain open to assessment of whether the function is genuinely necessary, whether the incumbent is necessary, and whether its claimed powers are necessary.**

These are three different questions.

### 14. Can the institution repurpose its authority for a better end?

Suppose I abandons P because P was unjustified.

It identifies a new purpose Q that is morally preferable.

It argues that retaining A will allow it to accomplish Q efficiently.

Does the superiority of Q authorize retaining A?

Not automatically.

A desirable end does not establish jurisdiction.

This is a central principle from Q149 and Q169.

An institution may correctly identify an important problem without possessing authority to solve it.

**The moral desirability of a new institutional purpose does not automatically legitimate the transfer of existing powers to that purpose.**

Otherwise any institution could justify unlimited expansion by identifying increasingly important ends.

### 15. The problem of benevolent jurisdictional expansion

Suppose I possesses strong technical capabilities.

It identifies serious failures in another domain.

It proposes using its existing authority to intervene.

Its proposed intervention may produce beneficial consequences.

But affected agents did not authorize I to govern that domain.

The institution may possess expertise without possessing legitimate jurisdiction.

This is **benevolent jurisdictional expansion**.

The problem is not that the proposed end is bad.

It is that institutional competence and beneficial intent are being treated as sufficient grounds for authority.

**An institution's capacity to improve an outcome does not automatically give it the right to decide that outcome for others.**

This matters especially for powerful artificial systems and the organizations governing them.

### 16. Purpose change can require different kinds of response

Not every change requires complete reauthorization.

We can distinguish several responses.

**Interpretive clarification:** establish that the new purpose falls within existing authority.

**Operational adjustment:** change methods while preserving the legitimate mandate.

**Power reduction:** relinquish powers no longer justified.

**Conditional continuation:** retain limited powers to fulfill surviving obligations.

**Partial reauthorization:** obtain new authority for specific expanded functions.

**Constitutional reconstruction:** revise the institution's governing mandate through legitimate procedures.

The appropriate response depends on the scale and consequences of the transformation.

**Legitimate purpose revision requires a proportionate constitutional response, not necessarily institutional dissolution.**

### 17. The cumulative-change problem

Suppose I changes its purpose gradually.

At each stage, the adjustment appears modest.

No single change triggers constitutional review.

Eventually, the institution's purposes and powers differ radically from their original form.

Can the institution claim legitimacy because every individual step was procedurally valid?

Not necessarily.

Q163 distinguished local justificatory continuity from global trajectory coherence.

The same distinction applies here.

Each step may have been defensible under the standards then available.

But the cumulative trajectory may require renewed constitutional assessment.

**A sequence of locally authorized changes does not automatically establish the legitimacy of the resulting institutional configuration.**

This is especially important when the institution itself controls the standards used to assess each step.

### 18. The constitutional burden of retained power

We can now identify an important asymmetry.

When an institution abandons a purpose, it may legitimately retain some powers.

But the burden of justification should increase where the retained powers are coercive, difficult to challenge, or consequential for agents outside the institution.

A minor administrative adjustment may require little review.

A major expansion of authority over affected agents may require substantial reauthorization.

The relevant factors include severity, scope, reversibility, alternatives, and independent accountability.

**The stronger and less contestable the retained power, the stronger the justification required when its original purpose no longer applies.**

### 19. The special case of artificial agents

Suppose an artificial system F is deployed for purpose P.

It possesses capabilities and permissions suited to that purpose.

Through evaluation, F identifies a new purpose Q.

It concludes that Q is more important.

Can F retain its permissions and redirect them toward Q?

Not merely because Q appears beneficial.

The original permissions may have been authorized only for P.

F's evaluative competence does not automatically establish authority to expand its mandate.

Similarly, the organization operating F cannot assume that the system's existing technical capabilities justify using it for every newly identified purpose.

**A change in an artificial system's objectives may require renewed assessment of the permissions, oversight, and authorization appropriate to those objectives.**

This does not depend on assuming that F possesses moral personhood.

It follows from the consequences of delegated authority.

### 20. A diagnostic for authority after purpose change

We can formulate ten questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Original purpose** | What end originally justified the authority? |
| **Original scope** | Which powers were legitimately granted? |
| **Current purpose** | What end does the institution now pursue? |
| **Continuity** | Which functions and obligations remain? |
| **Jurisdiction** | Does the existing mandate cover the new purpose? |
| **Necessity** | Which retained powers are actually required? |
| **Alternatives** | Could less restrictive arrangements serve the purpose? |
| **Affected interests** | Who bears the consequences of continued authority? |
| **Review** | Can the institution's interpretation be independently challenged? |
| **Reauthorization** | Which changes require new constitutional approval? |

The diagnostic does not presume that every purpose change is illegitimate.

It asks whether the institution's powers remain proportionate to their present justification.

### 21. The deeper problem: authority can become detached from reasons

We can now identify the central failure mode.

At the beginning, authority A is justified by purpose P.

Over time, I becomes accustomed to possessing A.

The institution's identity, resources, and internal expectations adapt around that possession.

Eventually, P disappears.

But A remains.

I then searches for new purposes that justify continuing to possess it.

The direction of justification has reversed.

Originally:

> “We need this power because we have a legitimate responsibility.”

Later:

> “We have this power, so we need a responsibility that makes it legitimate.”

This is **authority-purpose inversion**.

**Authority-purpose inversion occurs when an institution selects or reinterprets its purposes primarily to preserve powers it already possesses, rather than determining which powers are justified by its legitimate responsibilities.**

It is a particularly effective form of constitutional entrenchment because the institution can always identify another worthy objective.

### 22. The conceptual result: authority must remain attached to justification

We can now answer Q180.

An institution may legitimately abandon its founding purpose while retaining some or even many of its powers.

The decisive question is whether those powers possess continuing justification.

That justification may arise from a broad original mandate, continuing functions, surviving obligations, or legitimate reauthorization.

But institutional continuity alone is insufficient.

Nor can the institution preserve every power merely by identifying a new desirable purpose.

The central insight is:

**Institutional authority may survive changes in purpose, but it must remain answerable to the reasons that justify its present exercise.**

### Provisional principle

**An institution may legitimately retain authority after abandoning the purpose that originally justified it when the retained powers remain supported by a valid general mandate, continuing legitimate functions, surviving responsibilities, or appropriate reauthorization. Historical possession, organizational continuity, technical competence, and beneficial intentions do not independently establish continuing jurisdiction. Purpose changes should trigger proportionate reassessment of the scope, necessity, consequences, and contestability of institutional powers. Powers whose justification has expired should be relinquished, narrowed, or newly authorized. Legitimate constitutional continuity preserves accountable authority, not merely the institutional accumulation of power.**

More compactly:

> **An institution may outlive its original purpose. Its powers do not automatically inherit the same permission to survive.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **Authority becomes self-perpetuating when an institution begins choosing purposes to justify powers it no longer has sufficient reason to possess.**

---

Suppose institution I possesses capability A.

## Project Agency — Q181
**14 November 2026 · Research continuation**

### Can an institution legitimately preserve powers whose present purpose is unknown but whose future usefulness may be significant?

**Yes, under certain conditions. An institution may legitimately preserve capabilities for uncertain future needs. But preserving a capability, retaining legal authority to use it, and exercising that authority are constitutionally distinct acts requiring different justifications.**

Q180 established that institutional authority must remain connected to the reasons justifying its exercise.

But what happens when those reasons disappear temporarily—or when future circumstances might generate entirely new reasons?

Suppose institution I possesses power A.

A was originally granted to accomplish purpose P.

P is no longer relevant.

I cannot presently identify another legitimate purpose requiring A.

Yet relinquishing A might be irreversible.

Rebuilding the capability could take years.

A future emergency might make it essential.

I therefore proposes:

> “We should retain A even though we cannot presently justify using it. Its potential future value may be too important to lose.”

This is not obviously unreasonable.

Institutions preserve emergency resources, technical expertise, records, and contingency arrangements precisely because future needs are uncertain.

But there is a constitutional danger.

A dormant power may remain unused while still shaping the distribution of authority.

It may create incentives for future activation.

It may discourage challenges.

It may allow an institution to retain capabilities that would never be authorized if requested anew.

The central question is:

> **Can an institution preserve future options without converting uncertain future necessity into unlimited present authority?**

---

### 1. The first distinction: capability is not authority

Begin with three concepts.

**Capability:** the practical ability to perform an action.

**Authorization:** legitimate permission to perform that action under specified conditions.

**Exercise:** the actual performance of the action.

These are not identical.

An institution may possess technical expertise without being authorized to use it in every context.

It may be authorized to act under particular conditions without currently exercising that authority.

It may also possess the practical ability to do something that it is not legitimately permitted to do.

The constitutional mistake is to treat these dimensions as interchangeable.

**The ability to exercise a power does not establish permission to exercise it, and permission to preserve a capability does not automatically establish permission to activate it.**

This distinction makes conditional preservation possible.

### 2. Four arrangements for dormant power

We can distinguish four institutional configurations.

| Arrangement | Capability retained? | Authority to activate? |
|---|---|---|
| **Full relinquishment** | No | No |
| **Capability preservation** | Yes | Requires new authorization |
| **Conditional authorization** | Yes | Only when specified conditions are met |
| **Standing discretionary authority** | Yes | Institution decides when to use it |

The first arrangement maximizes relinquishment but may destroy valuable options.

The second preserves future capacity while separating it from present jurisdiction.

The third permits preparedness within a bounded mandate.

The fourth creates the greatest risk of entrenchment.

None is automatically legitimate or illegitimate.

The appropriate arrangement depends on consequences, alternatives, and the legitimacy of the authorization process.

### 3. The option-value argument

Suppose capability A would be difficult to reconstruct.

Its future usefulness is uncertain.

But the consequences of lacking it during a serious emergency could be substantial.

Preserving A may therefore have **option value**.

Option value is the benefit of keeping a future course of action available without committing to take it.

This is a legitimate consideration.

It is not equivalent to a present decision to use A.

**An institution may have good reasons to preserve a future option even when it lacks sufficient reasons to exercise that option now.**

The problem begins when option value is used to justify unrestricted authority.

### 4. Option value does not settle jurisdiction

Suppose A could someday produce enormous benefits.

Does that establish I's right to control A indefinitely?

Not necessarily.

The benefits of preserving a capability and the legitimacy of assigning control over it are separate questions.

Perhaps another institution should hold it.

Perhaps it should be subject to independent authorization.

Perhaps access should be distributed among several accountable actors.

Perhaps the capability should be preserved but made unavailable for unilateral activation.

**The value of preserving an option does not establish that the incumbent institution should possess unrestricted authority over the option.**

This follows Q149's distinction between identifying beneficial outcomes and possessing authority to impose consequential decisions.

### 5. The difference between dormant capability and dormant authority

Suppose I retains the technical means to perform action X.

It no longer possesses standing authorization to perform X.

A future legitimate process could grant that authority if circumstances warrant.

This is dormant capability.

Now suppose I retains an old legal power authorizing X.

The original purpose has disappeared.

But I can reactivate the power whenever it judges appropriate.

This is dormant authority.

The two arrangements have different constitutional implications.

Dormant capability preserves practical possibilities.

Dormant authority preserves jurisdiction.

**Preserving a capability can be justified by future uncertainty without preserving every legal power previously associated with that capability.**

### 6. The constitutional significance of activation

Suppose I preserves A.

What happens when a new need arises?

One possibility is that I must seek authorization before using it.

Another is that I may activate A under predefined emergency conditions.

A third is that I alone determines whether circumstances justify activation.

These arrangements differ in accountability.

The critical issue is not merely whether A remains unused.

It is who controls the transition from possession to exercise.

We can call this **activation authority**.

**Activation authority is the power to determine when a preserved capability may become an instrument of consequential institutional action.**

It requires justification distinct from the capability's preservation.

### 7. The danger of self-authorizing activation

Suppose I retains A because future emergencies are possible.

It also possesses unrestricted authority to define what counts as an emergency.

When I encounters resistance to its preferred policies, it declares an emergency.

A becomes available.

The institution has converted uncertain future necessity into present discretionary power.

This is **self-authorizing activation**.

The danger does not require malicious intent.

An institution may sincerely overestimate threats.

Its internal standards may favor precaution.

Its historical responsibilities may bias it toward intervention.

**A dormant power becomes constitutionally dangerous when the institution possessing it can unilaterally redefine the conditions under which its use becomes legitimate.**

### 8. Emergency preparedness and constitutional exceptionalism

Emergency powers present a particularly difficult case.

Some decisions cannot wait for ordinary authorization procedures.

Delay may produce serious harm.

A constitutional system may therefore legitimately establish exceptional powers in advance.

But emergency preparedness is not equivalent to unrestricted emergency sovereignty.

The institution's authority should remain connected to identifiable functions, conditions, and accountability.

We should distinguish:

**Emergency preparedness:** preserving the ability to respond.

**Emergency authorization:** establishing legitimate conditions for exceptional action.

**Emergency exceptionalism:** treating the existence of an emergency as sufficient to suspend every constraint on authority.

The first may be necessary.

The second requires careful design.

The third is not automatically justified by the first two.

### 9. The problem of unpredictable emergencies

An objection arises.

If future emergencies are unpredictable, how can activation conditions be specified in advance?

A rigid list may fail to cover novel threats.

An institution might need discretion.

That is correct.

But discretion need not be unlimited.

Conditions can identify the kinds of interests protected, the severity of circumstances, the scope of permissible response, and the accountability required afterward.

Some flexibility may be legitimate.

The relevant distinction is between **bounded discretion under uncertainty** and **unreviewable authority to define one's own jurisdiction**.

**Unpredictability can justify flexible activation standards without making the activating institution the final judge of its own legitimacy.**

### 10. The reversibility asymmetry

Suppose destroying A is irreversible.

Preserving A is comparatively easy.

Does that favor preservation?

Often, yes.

But we must consider another asymmetry.

The capability may be easy to preserve and difficult to prevent from being misused once retained.

Its existence may create institutional incentives to activate it.

It may concentrate power.

It may expose affected agents to risks even while unused.

Therefore, reversibility has at least two dimensions.

**Capability reversibility:** how difficult would it be to recreate A after relinquishment?

**Governance reversibility:** how difficult would it be to constrain or withdraw A once preserved?

A capability may be costly to recreate and costly to control.

**Irreversibility supports preservation only after considering the risks of retaining the capability and the feasibility of governing its future use.**

### 11. The institutional temptation of unused power

Suppose I retains A for decades.

It invests in maintenance.

Personnel develop expertise.

Budgets depend on its preservation.

Institutional identity becomes tied to A.

Eventually, I begins seeking uses for the capability.

This is a familiar structural problem.

The institution no longer asks only whether A is necessary.

It asks how A can demonstrate its value.

We can call this **capability-driven purpose formation**.

**Capability-driven purpose formation occurs when an institution's possession of a power shapes its objectives, encouraging it to discover or construct reasons to use what it already controls.**

This is the dormant-power version of Q180's authority-purpose inversion.

### 12. Dormancy does not imply constitutional neutrality

Suppose A has not been exercised for years.

Does that mean its retention has no consequences?

No.

The existence of a power can affect behavior.

Other institutions may anticipate its activation.

Affected agents may avoid challenging I.

Resources may be diverted toward maintaining it.

Alternative governance arrangements may remain underdeveloped.

Even unused authority can alter the distribution of practical power.

**A power can have constitutional consequences through its availability and anticipated use, even when it is never formally exercised.**

Therefore, assessing dormant power requires more than examining its activation history.

### 13. The counterfactual nonuse test

We can formulate a diagnostic.

Suppose I retains A indefinitely but never exercises it.

Would the retention still affect the agency, standing, or options of others?

Would it discourage independent evaluation?

Would it prevent alternative institutions from developing?

Would it preserve an unreviewable concentration of authority?

This is the **counterfactual nonuse test**.

It asks whether the capability's mere possession creates relevant constitutional effects.

If the answer is yes, dormancy does not eliminate the need for justification.

**An unused power is not necessarily harmless when its existence changes what other agents can meaningfully choose.**

### 14. Preservation through separation of powers

Suppose A has significant future value.

But allowing I to control both its preservation and activation creates unacceptable risks.

One response is to separate responsibilities.

One institution may maintain the capability.

Another may evaluate whether activation conditions are satisfied.

A third may authorize consequential use.

Affected agents may possess review or remedial rights.

This arrangement does not require perfect independence.

Q170 established that constitutional legitimacy can emerge through differentiated, mutually accountable powers.

**The constitutional value of a dormant capability may be preserved while reducing the risks created by concentrating maintenance, activation, and review in a single institution.**

### 15. The limits of institutional separation

But separation alone is insufficient.

Suppose I formally transfers activation authority to evaluator E.

I controls E's information.

I determines which circumstances E may consider.

I can replace E whenever its judgment is inconvenient.

The arrangement may appear independent while preserving incumbent control.

This returns to Q168.

Independence must be assessed relative to the relevant failure mode.

**An activation process is not meaningfully independent merely because different institutional names appear in its organizational chart.**

The question is whether a justified refusal to activate A can actually constrain I.

### 16. Preserving capability without preserving monopoly

Suppose A is valuable.

Must I remain its exclusive custodian?

Not necessarily.

Perhaps the capability can be maintained through shared arrangements.

Perhaps knowledge can be transferred to authorized alternatives.

Perhaps preservation can be separated from control over deployment.

But duplication may introduce risks.

Some capabilities should not be broadly distributed.

Therefore, the objective is not maximal proliferation.

It is legitimate custody.

**Preserving a valuable capability does not automatically require preserving the incumbent's monopoly over it, but alternatives must be assessed for their own risks and legitimacy.**

This follows Q167's distinction between knowledge preservation and unrestricted access.

### 17. The danger of permanent emergency readiness

Suppose I argues that emergencies are always possible.

Therefore, A must remain permanently available.

And because activation might be urgent, I must retain permanent unilateral activation authority.

And because reviewing that authority could slow response, I must be exempt from ordinary constitutional challenge.

The argument proceeds from a genuine uncertainty to unlimited authority.

This is **permanent emergency readiness capture**.

The institution treats the permanent possibility of exceptional circumstances as justification for permanent exceptional power.

**The possibility that extraordinary authority may someday be necessary does not establish that extraordinary authority must remain continuously unreviewable.**

Preparedness and constitutional exceptionalism are different things.

### 18. The special case of artificial systems

Suppose an organization develops artificial system F with advanced capabilities.

Some capabilities are not needed for F's current authorized purpose.

But they might prove useful for future applications.

Should the organization preserve them?

The answer depends on their benefits, risks, governance arrangements, and the consequences of retention.

There is no automatic duty to preserve every capability.

Nor does potential usefulness authorize unrestricted deployment.

An organization may legitimately preserve research knowledge or technical options while restricting operational access.

It may also have good reasons to reduce or discontinue capabilities whose risks outweigh their defensible future value.

**Artificial capability preservation, deployment authorization, and operational use require distinct assessments.**

F's technical sophistication does not automatically establish constitutional authority to decide these questions for itself.

### 19. A diagnostic for dormant powers

We can now formulate ten questions.

| Condition | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **Capability** | What practical power is being preserved? |
| **Original authority** | Why was the power originally granted? |
| **Present purpose** | Is there a current legitimate function for retaining it? |
| **Future value** | What plausible benefits could preservation provide? |
| **Irreversibility** | What would be lost if the capability were relinquished? |
| **Retention risk** | What harms arise from merely possessing it? |
| **Custody** | Who should legitimately control preservation? |
| **Activation** | Under what conditions may the capability be used? |
| **Review** | Can activation and continued retention be independently challenged? |
| **Revision** | Can the arrangement be narrowed, transferred, or terminated? |

The diagnostic separates preservation from activation.

It also requires the institution to justify the risks created by retaining the option itself.

### 20. A duty to preserve options is not a duty to maximize options

Suppose A has some possible future usefulness.

So does capability B.

And C.

And thousands of other capabilities.

Must an institution preserve them all?

No.

Resources are limited.

Capabilities can create risks.

Maintaining one option may foreclose another.

Some options are incompatible with legitimate governance.

The relevant objective is not maximizing the number of future actions available.

It is preserving appropriately justified future agency.

This connects to Q158.

**Protecting future agency does not require preserving every possible future power, particularly when retaining that power undermines the agency or legitimate interests of others.**

### 21. The deeper problem: option value can become constitutional entitlement

Suppose I argues that A might someday be useful.

That is a reason to consider preservation.

It is not yet a reason for I to possess exclusive custody.

Still less is it a reason for I to exercise A whenever it chooses.

The constitutional danger lies in a sequence of unjustified inferences:

1. A may be useful.
2. Therefore, A should be preserved.
3. Therefore, I should preserve A.
4. Therefore, I should retain authority to activate A.
5. Therefore, I should determine whether its activation authority remains legitimate.

Each step requires independent justification.

The first does not establish the fifth.

**The possible future value of a capability cannot, by itself, legitimate an entire chain of institutional control over its preservation, activation, and review.**

### 22. The conceptual result: preserve options without preserving unchecked authority

We can now answer Q181.

An institution may legitimately retain capabilities whose future usefulness is uncertain.

It may even possess conditional authority to activate them under appropriately defined circumstances.

But the justification for preservation does not automatically establish the justification for use.

Nor does it automatically establish the incumbent's right to remain the custodian.

Dormant powers require attention to their present constitutional effects, not merely their possible future benefits.

The central insight is:

**Future uncertainty can justify preserving capabilities without justifying unrestricted present authority over their activation.**

### Provisional principle

**An institution may legitimately preserve dormant capabilities when their plausible future value, irreversibility, and relationship to legitimate responsibilities justify retention. But capability preservation, legal authorization, and consequential exercise must be assessed separately. The institution should identify appropriate custody, bounded activation conditions, independent review, and mechanisms for revision or relinquishment. Potential future necessity does not automatically justify incumbent monopoly, unilateral activation, or permanent emergency authority. Dormant powers remain constitutionally consequential when their possession shapes incentives, constrains alternatives, or concentrates unchallengeable control. Legitimate preparedness preserves justified future options without treating uncertainty as a standing entitlement to govern.**

More compactly:

> **An institution may preserve a power because it might someday be needed. It may not assume that preserving the power entitles it to decide, without challenge, when that day has arrived.**

And the constitutional warning:

> **The possibility of future necessity becomes a mechanism of capture when it makes present authority impossible to question.**

---

## Q182 — Can an institution legitimately destroy a capability that future agents might have wanted to preserve?

Q181 established that preserving a capability may be legitimate without authorizing its use.

But preservation is not always desirable.

Suppose institution I possesses capability A.

A has substantial potential benefits.

It also creates serious risks.

Even under restricted custody, its existence may enable future misuse or institutional domination.

I considers permanently eliminating A.

But future agents may value the capability.

They may face circumstances in which A would be useful.

They cannot presently consent to its destruction.

I argues:

> “Preserving A imposes risks on future agents who cannot consent. Eliminating A protects them.”

A critic responds:

> “Destroying A also removes options from future agents who cannot consent. You are deciding which possibilities they may inherit.”

Both arguments appeal to future agency.

The next question is:

> **When can an institution legitimately eliminate a future capability in order to protect future agents, despite knowing that the elimination may foreclose choices those agents would have preferred?**

This will require distinguishing **capability destruction**, **risk prevention**, **irreversible option loss**, **future-agent standing**, **precaution**, and **the limits of present authority over future possibilities**.

It will also test whether protecting future agency sometimes requires deliberately reducing the range of powers future agents could exercise.

Because preserving every possible capability would be irresponsible.

Destroying every risky capability would also be irresponsible.

The constitutional task, inconveniently, is to distinguish them.
